Air pollution and climate change impact on respiratory health in Africa: Evidence and interventions
items.source_name: Journal of the Pan African Thoracic Society
items.summary_raw: Air pollution and climate change are global environmental health challenges impacting human respiratory health. In Africa, air pollution compounded by climate change is an important risk factor affecting respiratory health from early life and across the life course. While a lack of epidemiological data underestimates the burden of exposures and the resulting health implications, there is growing evidence that explores these interactions. In this narrative review, we aim to explore the interplay of air pollution and climate change on respiratory health, focusing on vulnerable African populations, with the purpose of spotlighting African studies and cohorts exploring these impacts. Furthermore, we review some of the interventions studied to address the negative impacts and additionally offer a way forward to address some of these issues.

items.title: Initial affect shapes risk-benefit information processing and public support for carbon dioxide removal technologies
items.summary_raw: Abstract Given the accelerating climate crisis, carbon dioxide removal (CDR) technologies are becoming increasingly important, while public support may play a relevant role in their implementation. This support is influenced by how citizens inform themselves about the technology. While prior research has examined public support under conditions of no or predefined information provision, little is known about the factors that shape how individuals actively select information about CDR and integrate it into their preferences about the technology. Here, we investigate how initial affect towards CDR shapes laypersons’ selection and evaluation of benefit-related versus risk-related information about the technology and how these processes influence subsequent policy support. In a preregistered study with 714 U.S. participants, we introduced a novel information-sampling task, in which participants could freely choose which information about CDR to attend to, followed by a policy choice experiment assessing public support of CDR technologies. In line with our hypotheses, participants’ initial affect influenced their information search: more initial positive affect towards CDR was associated with a higher likelihood to select benefit-related versus risk-related information about CDR. This confirmatory information search, in turn, was associated with immediate changes in affect towards the technology, especially when the information was perceived as persuasive. These affective changes…

items.title: The power of the past: Temporal framing enhances gender‐inclusive language support among conservatives
items.source_name: Analyses of Social Issues and Public Policy
items.summary_raw: Abstract The singular they is commonly used in English as a form of gender‐inclusive language. Despite its potential to contribute to gender equality, gender‐inclusive language is often met with resistance, primarily from political conservatives. Arguments against the use of the singular they include rejection of language change and appeals to tradition. Such arguments fit with conservatives’ nostalgic focus on the past. Thus, we investigate whether conservatives’ support for the singular they can be increased by past‐focused temporal framing that presents the singular they as consistent with the past and thereby appeals to conservatives’ nostalgic focus on the past. In an online experiment, U.S. American participants ( N = 377) indicated their endorsement of either a past‐focused or a future‐focused message promoting the singular they and their personal use of the singular they . Consistent with predictions, the more conservative participants were, the lower their endorsement and use of the singular they . However, the effect of political ideology on endorsement was attenuated by the past‐focused compared to the future‐focused message. Singular they use was not affected by temporal framing. Collective nostalgia was associated with conservatism but was not identified as an underlying mechanism of the temporal focus effect. The present findings suggest that past‐focused temporal framing has the potential to increase conservatives’ support for the singular they and, thereby…

items.title: ‘Not in my backyard’ or ‘Not in our backyard’? The influence of spatial proximity and regional belonging on attitudes and opinion expression on site selection for a nuclear waste repository
items.summary_raw: New energy infrastructure is often met with a so-called ‘not-in-my-backyard’ mentality in local residents. While much research on this topic has focused on renewable energies, little is known about the factors influencing public opinion on where to host deep geological repositories for high-level radioactive waste. Thus, this study conducts two experiments to investigate the effects of two potential explanatory factors and how they interact in a representative sample of German residents (N = 3015). Drawing on the literature on the ‘not-in-my-backyard’ mentality, the first experiment reveals that higher spatial proximity – i.e., a smaller distance in kilometers between a person's place of residence and the potential location of a nuclear waste repository – increases individuals' perceived personal relevance of the hosting decision. However, the second experiment shows that this effect is conditioned by regional belonging . While feeling affected by the hosting decision decreases for spatially distant sites that are located outside a person's own region, perceived relevance remains high when spatially distant sites are still located within a person's own region. Furthermore, mediation analysis reveals that this moderation effect also translates into stronger opposition against the decision and a higher likelihood for individuals' opinion expression even if the site is located further away. Future research should therefore extend the idea of ‘not-in-my-backyard (NIMBY)’ and…

items.title: Theoretical Analysis of the Relationship Between Climate Change and Sustainable Development
items.source_name: International Journal of Accounting, Finance, Auditing, Management and Economics
items.summary_raw: The adoption of the Paris Agreement and the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development has made the relationship between climate change and sustainable development a centre of interest for researchers. This work aims to analyse the theoretical dimensions that govern this relationship. For that reason, a systematic literature review was conducted following the PRISMA protocol, based on 17 selected peer-reviewed scientific papers. Content analysis was carried out using QualCoder software; the analysis reveals that the climate change–sustainable development relationship is overwhelmingly framed by the conceptual dyad of synergies and trade-offs (n=53 occurrences in a text passage) and systematically co-occurs in the same passages (n=16 co-occurrences). Furthermore, the code integration appears (n=15 occurrences) and is situated in opposition to the code separation. The relationship is primarily framed at local and national spatial scales. Additionally, concrete policy and research operationalisation have no occurrences in the text. Finally, the moderate quality of the selected articles, the limited size of the corpus, and the fact that the coding was performed individually are limitations of the study. This work represents an integrated conceptual mapping of the theoretical relationship; it adopts a coding framework that distinguishes it from previous work JEL Classification: Q54, Q01, Q56 Paper type: systematic literature review with a theoretical focus

items.title: Attitudes towards pain relief and wound management, and their on-farm use during cattle dehorning in northern Australia
items.summary_raw: Context Dehorning remains a common procedure across the northern Australian beef industry due to the widespread use of horned breeds and management constraints in extensive operations. Amputation dehorning has cattle welfare and production implications, including haemorrhage, infection, flystrike, weight loss and mortality. The use of and producer attitudes towards pain relief and wound treatments are not well documented. Aims This study aimed to document cattle dehorning practices in northern Australia and identify producer-defined priorities for effective wound management treatments in extensive beef systems. Methods An online survey targeting Australian beef cattle producers was conducted between February and August 2023. Four online focus groups involving producers and industry stakeholders from northern Australia were conducted to explore attitudes, practices, experiences, and priorities related to pain relief and wound management for dehorning of cattle. Quantitative data were analysed using Fisher’s exact test and qualitative data were analysed thematically. Key results Dehorning was performed by 92.5% of northern Australian survey respondents, most commonly using surgical methods. Pain relief was used by 75% of producers, most commonly Tri Solfen® (65%) and meloxicam (28%). Multimodal analgesia was used by only a minority (15%). Relief from pain (91%) and improved wound healing (74%) were the most common perceived benefits of pain relief, with efficacy (87%) and…

items.title: Review sustainable energy from livestock waste: a review of biogas production pathways
items.summary_raw: The growing demand for sustainable energy and the environmental challenges of livestock waste management have intensified interest in biogas as a renewable and circular bioenergy solution. This review critically evaluates biogas production from key livestock wastes such as chicken manure, piggery waste, and cow dung focusing on how feedstock composition, anaerobic digestion pathways, pretreatment methods, and co-digestion strategies influence methane yield and process stability. These substrates differ markedly in biochemical characteristics: chicken manure is nitrogen-rich and prone to ammonia inhibition, piggery waste exhibits high biodegradability and methane potential, and cow dung provides stable digestion but is constrained by lignocellulosic hydrolysis limitations. Comparative analysis of experimental studies reveals wide variability in reported methane yields, driven by differences in operating conditions, reactor design, microbial adaptation, and scale. Persistent gaps between theoretical biomethane potential and experimental performance are discussed, highlighting the roles of ammonia toxicity, hydrolysis-limited kinetics, and scale-dependent losses. Co-digestion and pretreatment consistently enhance methane production by improving nutrient balance and substrate accessibility, yet challenges remain in methodological standardization, process scalability, and long-term operational stability. Key research gaps include limited integration of microbial community…

items.title: The Nuclear Company Unveils a Chinese-Style Reactor Megaproject in Kentucky
items.summary_raw: After decades of stagnation, the nuclear industry has drummed up all kinds of ideas meant to revive the prospects for building reactors in the United States. Make the reactors smaller. Micro , even! Cool them with helium or molten salt instead of water. Invite the Koreans or Canadians to come teach us how to construct atomic power stations again. Yet the startup bold enough to name itself The Nuclear Company launched in 2024 on a simpler thesis: Just go with the large-scale reactors we have built before, and construct them in bulk to bring down costs. Essentially, do what the Chinese did. While the U.S. struggled for 15 years to complete its first two Westinghouse AP1000s, the 1.1-gigawatt units designed at the dawn of this century to be America’s flagship nuclear technology, China built four in the same time period. Beijing then reverse-engineered the technology to make its own version with an entirely domestic supply chain. China now has 10 operating Hualong One reactors and at least 37 more on the way. The U.S. ultimately completed its first two AP1000s at Southern Company’s Alvin W. Vogtle Electric Generating Plant in eastern Georgia right around the same time. The Nuclear Company was formed by hiring former managers who oversaw the Georgia project. Despite the Trump administration’s pledge to finance construction of at least 10 more large nuclear reactors, the only projects that have broken ground are new, first-of-a-kind small modular reactors that skeptics fear will…

items.title: Macromolecular association creates dispersity of components that determines liquid–liquid phase separation of oppositely charged polyions
items.summary_raw: Developing insight into liquid–liquid phase separation in complex polyelectrolyte mixtures has acquired new urgency considering the role this process plays in the formation of biomolecular condensates, which are involved in diverse processes including, stress response, signal transduction, metabolism, gene regulation, and many human diseases. Condensates can be viewed as a biological membraneless structure situated, in scale and function, between macromolecules and cells. The physical properties of, and the physico-chemical environments within, condensates are very important determinants of their biological function. These properties and environments are determined by the phase separation process. Earlier experimental work in one of our laboratories characterized in detail a phase separation process in solutions of oppositely charged polypeptides. Considering new information being developed on macromolecular association in homogeneous solutions of oppositely charged polyions, we have revisited our earlier data looking into the influence of intermolecular association on the outcome of the phase transition. Such influence is clearly established in this Brief Report. We demonstrate that dispersity of species in homogeneous solution owing to macromolecular association affects phase separation by creating an open miscibility gap, leading to a dependence of the phase compositions on the initial polymer volume fraction. It is very likely that this plays a significant role in the…

items.title: Anomalous narrow-band correlation in a natural superconducting heterostructure
items.summary_raw: A new frontier in condensed matter physics is to stack atomically thin layered materials with different properties and create intriguing phenomena which do not exist in any of the constituent layers. Transition metal dichalcogenide 4Hb-TaS 2, with an alternating stacking of a spin liquid candidate 1T-TaS 2 and a superconductor 1H-TaS 2 , is a natural heterostructure for such a purpose. Recently, rare phenomena were indeed observed, including chiral superconductivity, two-component nematic superconductivity, topological surface superconductivity, and enigmatic magnetic memory. A widely proposed starting point to understand such a mysterious heterostructure requires strong electronic correlation, presumably provided by 1T-TaS 2 layers with a narrow flat band near the Fermi level (E F ). Here, by using angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy, we reveal the theoretically expected flat band near E F in the energy-momentum space. However, this flat band only exists on the 1T-TaS 2 terminated surface layer with broken translational symmetry, but not on the 1T-TaS 2 subsurface layers buried in the bulk. These results directly challenge the foundation of the current theoretical paradigm. On the 1T-TaS 2 terminated surface layer, we further revealed a pseudogap and an anomalous doping effect. These phenomena and the dichotomy between surface and bulk layers also shed light on the unusual coexistence of distinct electronic orders in this mysterious heterostructure.

items.title: Translational control of microglial metabolism, inflammatory responses, and survival by the eIF4E-binding proteins
items.summary_raw: In Alzheimer’s disease (AD), activation of the mechanistic target of rapamycin (mTOR) pathway promotes microglial neuroprotective functions by engaging multiple cell receptors. However, the relevant downstream effectors are not fully understood. mTOR complex 1 (mTORC1) promotes mRNA translation by phosphorylating and inactivating eukaryotic translation initiation factor 4E-binding protein 1 and 2 (4E-BP1/2), which are expressed in microglia. 4E-BP1 levels in cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) are elevated in AD and correlate with markers of microglial reactivity and disease progression. Using linear regression analysis, we found that elevated CSF 4E-BP1 levels strengthen the association between soluble TREM2 levels and neurodegeneration in amyloid-positive individuals. To investigate the underlying mechanism, we performed in vitro experiments demonstrating that amyloid-β inactivated 4E-BP1 in murine microglia. The mTOR-mediated inactivation is highly dependent on Spleen Tyrosine Kinase (SYK) signaling and repeated exposure to amyloid-β impaired this process, whereas prolonged exposure increased 4E-BP1 levels in microglia. Deletion of 4E-BP1/2 resulted in increased mitochondrial mass and oxidative phosphorylation, reduced pro-inflammatory signaling, and protected microglia from amyloid-induced apoptosis. Thus, impaired 4E-BP1 inactivation—due to reduced mTOR signaling or excess 4E-BP1—disrupts immune resolution, leading to metabolic exhaustion and microglial cell death. We identify…

items.title: Molecular fossils of an ancestral code revealed by large-scale analysis of tRNAs
items.summary_raw: Modern tRNAs are thought to have evolved from simpler RNA minihelices resembling acceptor stems, some of which could be specifically aminoacylated. A central and testable prediction of minihelix-based models is that vestiges of ancestral coding relationships should remain embedded within the acceptor stems of contemporary tRNAs and should persist after correction for structural constraints. Here, we ask whether cognate anticodon-like triplets are statistically enriched in nonanticodon regions of modern tRNAs beyond what would be expected from structural and compositional constraints alone. Using a curated dataset of 77,335 canonical tRNA sequences and a structure-aware statistical framework, we find that for a subset of amino acids cognate anticodon-like triplets are significantly enriched in acceptor stems and, to a lesser extent, in other structural domains. Notably, these amino acids include those previously shown to support specific minihelix aminoacylation [Y. M. Hou, P. Schimmel, Nature 333 , 140–145 (1988); C. Francklyn, P. Schimmel, Nature 337 , 478–481 (1989)]. The strongest acceptor-stem signals survive structure-preserving null models, and cluster nonrandomly against proposed chronologies of amino acid incorporation into the genetic code. Together, these findings identify molecular fossils within modern tRNAs consistent with the persistence of an ancestral operational code, and provide refined statistical support for the notion that extant codon–amino acid…

items.title: Comparative analysis of photocatalytic, enzymatic, and chemical approaches to identify canonical and noncanonical surfaceomes
items.summary_raw: The cell surface is a critical nexus in cellular communication and a rich landscape yielding the majority of current therapeutic targets, yet only a small fraction of cell surface proteins have been targeted therapeutically. The cell surface proteome (surfaceome) comprises only ~1% of the human proteome by mass, motivating enrichment strategies to detect surfaceome alterations in disease for drug target discovery. Developments in photocatalytic technology have revolutionized the study of protein neighborhoods around specific targets of interest, but photocatalysis has been underutilized for global surfaceome analysis. Here, we describe five distinct photocatalytic surfaceomics strategies, all without the need for cellular engineering, that apply the photocatalyst Eosin Y attached to different cell surface structures: direct glycan ligation, glycan attachment via two different lectins, membrane insertion, and free in extracellular space. We systematically compare these photocatalytic surfaceomics methods to each other as well as to three established chemical and enzymatic surfaceomics methods. We demonstrate that the different photocatalytic surfaceomics techniques achieve broadly similar canonical cell surface protein enrichment but show some important differences reflective of cell surface attachment mechanism. These mechanistically orthogonal surfaceomics techniques consistently identified numerous nonglycosylated proteins with high concordance, many of which represent an…

items.title: Enhancing simulations of disordered protein ensembles with chemical shift restraints in coarse-grained models
items.summary_raw: With more than one third of the human proteome being structurally disordered, intrinsically disordered proteins (IDPs) are key contributors to complex cellular functions, despite their highly dynamic conformational ensembles remaining elusive to conventional techniques in structural biology. Coarse-grained (CG) simulation methods thus serve as a gold standard to refine IDP ensembles. These methods, when relying on elastic network models or rigid body to sample secondary structure, are however inherently limited in their capability to model and sample transient secondary structure at a residue-level resolution as informed by experimental data. This fundamental limitation persists despite experimental evidence suggesting that transient structural propensities are a fundamental hallmark of IDP function. Through an artificial neural network capable of predicting backbone chemical shifts from C α -only protein conformations, we present a generalized framework which does not rely on dihedral parameterization to equip one bead-per-aminoacid CG force fields with the ability to sample functional elements of secondary structure. When applied on a large set of IDPs in isolation or condensates, our approach correctly recapitulates both local and global arrangements, yielding experimentally informed ensembles that can inform structure-mediated function and resolve force field limitations. This can yield a fruitful exploration of ensemble-to-function relationships in IDPs, allowing to…

items.title: Gene conversion is a key driver of diversity hotspots in Mycobacterium tuberculosis antigens and virulence-associated loci
items.summary_raw: Despite the long-held view of Mycobacterium tuberculosis ( Mtb ) as a genetically conserved pathogen, many genomic regions remain poorly resolved due to high sequence homology and repetitive content. Using complete genome assemblies generated from long-read sequencing of 151 globally representative clinical isolates, we comprehensively analyzed genome-wide patterns of genetic diversity and evolution across the Mtb genome. Our analysis uncovers pronounced diversity hotspots within paralogous regions (PRs) generated by recurrent gene conversion between homologous genes. In many cases, these hotspots exhibit more than an order of magnitude greater genetic diversity than the rest of the Mtb genome, which is otherwise characterized by remarkably low variation. Mutations within these regions display clustered substitution patterns, excess paralog-matching variants, and distinct mutational spectra consistent with ongoing gene conversion. Our analysis identifies over 300 individual gene conversion events (GCEs) distributed throughout the Mtb phylogeny. These GCEs occur predominantly within gene families associated with virulence and host–pathogen interactions, including the PE, PPE, and ESX families. Several of the most pronounced diversity hotspots occur in antigens encoded within PRs. Among these, the vaccine candidate PPE18 harbors mutations in validated epitope sequences and predicted alterations in HLA-II binding. Together, these findings demonstrate that gene conversion…

items.title: Unveiling the structure of Leishmania flagella through cryoelectron tomography
items.summary_raw: Leishmania are unicellular parasites that cause the serious disease leishmaniasis, presenting ongoing global challenges as existing treatments face issues with resistance and toxicity. Leishmania contain a single motile flagellum, essential for transmission, which has the conserved [9 + 2] microtubule arrangement. We used cryoelectron tomography to determine the ultrastructure of the Leishmania tarentolae 96-nm repeat and paraflagellar rod. While the overall structure, including three broad radial spokes and two-headed outer dynein arms, resembles other eukaryotes like Trypanosoma brucei, Tetrahymena, and Opisthokonts, the Leishmania flagellum also exhibits unique and asymmetrical features. These include asymmetrically shaped radial spoke heads similar to T. brucei , suggesting this may represent a kinetoplastid-specific feature. Further, Leishmania contain an additional inner-junction and 8-nm wide A2 protofilament hole. Strikingly, Leishmania have many doublet-specific structures such as outer dynein arm tethers, interdoublet linkers, and heterogeneous connections to the paraflagellar rod. In this work, we show that divergent structural traits of Leishmania flagella highlight lineage-specific adaptations within eukaryotes.

items.title: Structure of a sparsely populated chimeric intermediate that facilitates fold-switching of a metamorphic protein
items.summary_raw: Metamorphic proteins challenge the single-sequence-structure-function paradigm by switching between distinct folds that often adopt complementary functions. However, the conformational states sampled along the fold-switching pathway have remained elusive because they are transient and unstable. Using multinuclear chemical exchange saturation transfer and relaxation dispersion NMR, combined with chemical shift–based structure determination and protein engineering, we visualized the atomic resolution structure of an “invisible” state of the metamorphic chemokine lymphotactin. This state is a chimera that integrates the secondary and tertiary structure of one fold with the quaternary assembly of the other. Locking lymphotactin into a single conformation abolishes access to this state, supporting its role as an on-pathway intermediate in metamorphosis. The stabilization of such hybrid intermediates is likely to have facilitated the evolution of fold-switching and represents a powerful strategy for protein design.

items.title: Multi-omics and spatial analysis of microgravity-grown glioblastoma organoids reveal superior modeling of advanced disease after long-term spaceflight
items.summary_raw: Creating accurate organoid models remains a challenge, particularly for diseases like glioblastoma (GBM), an aggressive, treatment-resistant brain cancer with an immunosuppressive microenvironment. To overcome limitations of Earth-based models (sedimentation and disaggregation) and leverage the unique advantages of space (accelerated disease progression and immune dysregulation), this study utilizes a panel of GBM-myeloid organoids cultured for 40 d aboard the International Space Station. Spaceflight-grown GBM organoids have more uniform morphology compared to ground controls. We observed a context-dependent response to spaceflight, with the inclusion of macrophages and monocytes altering the bulk and spatial transcriptional response. While GBM-alone organoids have transcriptional markers of less aggressive disease in microgravity, organoids containing GBM cells + monocytes have increased expression of genes associated with disease progression and poor patient outcomes. Gene expression patterns are more spatially organized, with mesenchymal-related genes enriched in the core and inflammation-related genes enriched at the periphery, mimicking GBM tumor architecture. Microgravity-grown GBM+monocyte organoids exhibit increased secretion of proteins such as CXCL12 and LOX-1, associated with more aggressive disease. Infrared chemical imaging confirms spatial chemical gradients of DNA, protein, and lipid species in both space- and terrestrially-grown organoids. In summary, this…

items.title: Mitochondrial subpopulations promote cellular responses to changes in metabolic demand and signal transduction
items.summary_raw: When mammalian cells are under increased ATP demand, mitochondria segregate into two distinct subpopulations, one capable of oxidative phosphorylation (oxidative subpopulation) and another specialized in reductive synthesis of metabolic precursors (reductive subpopulation). Here we report that mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) along with protein components of the mitochondrial nucleoid segregate to the oxidative subpopulation in response to increased ATP demand. This suggests that formation of the reductive mitochondrial subpopulation might serve to eliminate alternative uses of mitochondrial NAD(P)H when cells are under bioenergetic or nutrient stress. To examine this further, we studied mitochondria in cells exposed to low levels of glutamine. Mitochondria use glutaminase (GLS1) to maintain net glutamine uptake when cytosolic glutamine decreases, by converting glutamine to glutamate. The resulting glutamate can either be oxidized into α-ketoglutarate to enter the TCA cycle or utilized in the reductive synthesis of proline/ornithine. GLS1 can polymerize into hyperactive filaments in response to elevations in inorganic phosphate as might occur when ATP consumption exceeds production. However, when extracellular glutamine is reduced, GLS1 filaments segregated away from mtDNA, becoming colocalized with pyrroline-5-carboxylate synthase (P5CS) filaments in reductive mitochondria lacking ATP synthase markers. This cosegregation supported the ability of TGF-β signaling to enhance…

items.title: Harry L. Swinney: Nonlinear science and chaos pioneer
items.summary_raw: Harry Leonard Swinney passed away peacefully at his home in Austin, Texas, on July 13, 2026, at the age of 87. Harry was an exceptional experimental physicist, well-known for elegant studies of instabilities, nonlinear dynamics, chaos and pattern formation in a wide variety of fluid, chemical, and granular systems, work whose influence propagated into numerous scientific and engineering disciplines well beyond the particular problems that prompted it. The late Russell Donnelly of the University of Oregon used to say, “Harry is a prince”; Russ meant it, in the spirit of the tenth-century Persian poet Ferdowsi, as a compliment affirming the nobility, dignity, integrity, and grace with which Harry pursued his science and treated everyone he worked alongside.

items.title: In-cloud motions shape warm-rain production in marine clouds: Evidence from multiyear observations
items.summary_raw: Despite years of research, the processes controlling warm-rain formation remain uncertain. Leveraging multiple years of observations collected across four oceanic regions, we systematically reassess the properties of precipitation just beneath cloud base. The observations show that warm-rain characteristics are remarkably consistent within cloud regimes yet differ substantially between stratocumulus and cumulus, indicating that cloud-regime properties exert a stronger influence on warm precipitation than regional environmental variability. Precipitation is observed beneath marine stratocumulus in over 56% of cloudy columns with liquid water path (LWP) <130 g m −2 , rising to more than 84% in columns with LWP beyond 130 g m −2 . This indicates that marine stratocumulus routinely support warm-rain formation and suggests that barriers to precipitation onset in this regime are weaker than commonly assumed. For the same LWP, oceanic cumulus precipitate less frequently than stratocumulus but on average produce two times larger and one to two orders of magnitude fewer precipitation drops. This contrast is consistent with cumulus presenting two times stronger updrafts and lower adiabaticity than stratocumulus, both of which can affect drop growth histories. Whereas the precipitation characteristics of stratocumulus are generally consistent with growth by collision–coalescence during gravitational free fall in low LWP clouds, those of cumulus cannot be explained without invoking…

items.title: Compensation of the effects of temperature on a motor system in the crab, Cancer borealis
items.summary_raw: Understanding how warming affects life-critical physiological processes is increasingly important as ocean temperatures rise at unprecedented rates. We study the stomatogastric system of the crab Cancer borealis . Movement depends on multiple temperature-sensitive processes, from motor pattern generation to neuromuscular transmission and contraction. Previous studies examined these levels separately and showed that warming increased pyloric rhythm frequency until the rhythm crashed at extreme temperatures. Here, we examined how the neuromuscular transform responds to this increase in motor neuron activity. We simultaneously recorded motor neuron activity, muscle fiber membrane potential, and contraction force. As temperature increased, the pyloric rhythm frequency increased, the excitatory junctional potential amplitudes remained constant, and muscle contraction diminished and failed. When muscles were stimulated at a fixed low frequency mimicking neuronal activity at cold temperatures, contraction decreased with acute warming. Increasing motor nerve stimulation frequency to mimic neuronal activity at warm temperatures partially rescued contraction. This shows that the temperature-dependent increase in neuronal firing provides partial compensation but is insufficient to prevent the loss of contraction at high temperatures. Because warming hyperpolarized muscle fibers, it moved the membrane potential further from the contraction threshold, and decreased synaptic integration…

items.title: Validation of targets linked to weight gain in C57BL/6 mice and translational aspects in humans
items.summary_raw: Obesity is linked to complex interactions between an organism’s genetic background and its environment. Mouse models have been invaluable research tools to study obesity, with C57BL/6N being widely studied, given its propensity for weight gain on a high-fat diet (HFD). Despite this, the genetic basis of its susceptibility is poorly understood. In a partner paper we have identified SNP variants in 11 genes causing susceptibility to, or protection against, HFD-induced obesity in male C57BL/6N mice explaining 87% of the individual variation in fat gain. Surprisingly, most of them were maximally expressed outside the brain. In this study, we further validate some of these targets. We demonstrate that tissue-specific inhibition of Nova1 and Mchr1 in muscle, Nr1i3 in liver, and Ahr in lung and liver led to resistance to HFD–induced obesity or glucose intolerance. Further RNAseq analysis revealed that mTOR, Acox1, IL-15, and eIF2a signals are positioned downstream of these genes, potentially mediating their effects on obesity susceptibility. Importantly, variants in eight of the genes identified here have been previously implicated in human obesity, suggesting that a deeper understanding of the genetic/environment interactions of model systems can inform this complex human disease. Our work confirms that body fat regulation is likely more complex than current models which focus on the brain–adipose axis suggest.

items.title: Signal peptides for engineered protein secretion by free and hydrogel-encapsulated cyanobacteria
items.summary_raw: Cyanobacteria provide a promising platform for light-driven heterologous protein production. In heterologous production systems, cells are typically lysed for product purification or to facilitate interaction with external substrates, unless the product is secreted. Fusion to molecular “shipping labels” known as signal peptides can target chimeric proteins to native membrane translocation pathways and result in secretion. In this work, we identified signal peptides from the model cyanobacterium Synechococcus elongatus PCC 7942 ( S. elongatus ) and genetically fused to two heterologous enzymes: the reporter nanoluciferase (NLuc) and an oxidative laccase (CotA). Increased extracellular activity was observed for one or more signal-protein variants for both enzymes. Furthermore, cells of S. elongatus producing a signal-laccase chimera were encapsulated within an alginate hydrogel, and the resulting engineered living material released sufficient enzyme to decolorize a dye pollutant in its surroundings. These findings streamline recombinant protein production in cyanobacteria and facilitate environmental interactions with cell products, expanding the potential applications of both free-living and material-encapsulated cyanobacteria.

items.title: C1ql2 gates stress vulnerability by regulating microglia-mediated synaptic pruning in the BLA-vHPC circuit
items.summary_raw: Synaptic remodeling in emotional circuits contributes to the development of stress-related emotional disorders. However, such remodeling generally exhibits considerable heterogeneity across specific neuronal populations and the underlying molecular mechanisms remain poorly understood. Here, we identified C1ql2 as a key molecular regulator that governs projection-specific synaptic vulnerability within basolateral amygdala (BLA). Transcriptional profiling revealed that C1ql2 expression is enriched in BLA neurons projecting to ventral hippocampus (BLA →vHPC PNs), but not in those projecting to nucleus accumbens (NAc), and is significantly down-regulated following chronic social defeat stress (CSDS). Gain- and loss-of-function manipulations demonstrated that C1ql2 regulates stress-induced neuronal remodeling in BLA →vHPC PNs, including dendritic hypertrophy, synaptic outgrowth, and enhanced glutamatergic transmission, thereby shaping susceptibility to anxiety-like behavior. We further found that CSDS-induced C1ql2 loss impairs microglial engulfment of BLA →vHPC PNs synapses, leading to aberrant synaptic accumulation. Our findings establish C1ql2-mediated neuron-microglia cross talk that critically regulates circuit-specific synaptic pathophysiology in stress-related disorders.

items.title: Naturalistic spatial education engages distinct neural processes for mental rotation, cognitive load, and linguistic demands
items.summary_raw: Neuroscience studies typically isolate spatial cognition using simplified tasks targeting a single cognitive process. However, during formal spatial education, the brain rarely performs one cognitive operation at a time. Here, we used functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) to assess neural systems involved in dynamically processing an educational spatial visualization lesson. We quantified lesson content using an instructional-design framework capturing variation in spatial complexity, cognitive load, and verbal density. We then characterized how instructional demands modulated brain function using content-evoked responses, functional connectivity, and network-centrality. Spatial transformations during instruction robustly recruited parietal and premotor regions, which were linearly modulated by spatial complexity. This parietal dominance aligns with theories that these areas encode geometric and quantitative dimensions. In contrast, domain-general frontal activity tracked overall processing demands, and language regions tracked verbal density. Activity also varied with learners’ spatial abilities: higher spatial performers showed stronger modulation of parietal and premotor regions as spatial demands increased, and greater domain-general modulation across content types. Thus, the same circuitry representing spatial transformations during instruction also reflects individual variation in spatial cognition. Parietal regions showed the highest centrality and strongest…

items.title: CD28 costimulation is organized by signaling condensates and counteracted by PD-1
items.summary_raw: T cell activation relies on the coordinated integration of T cell receptor (TCR) and cosignaling pathways, yet how these signals are physically organized remains unclear. Here, we demonstrate that CD28 co-stimulation is driven by a condensation mechanism in which the CD28 intracellular domain (ICD) forms signaling condensates with the Src-family kinase Lck. Ligand engagement promotes CD28 ICD accessibility and triggers rapid CD28/Lck condensation, enhancing CD28 phosphorylation, cytoskeletal polarization, and cytokine production. The downstream effectors of CD28, including PI3K and GRB2, can also be recruited into the CD28-Lck condensates in our reconstituted system. We further identify PD-1 as a graded regulator of this process: Monophosphorylated PD-1 is recruited into CD28/Lck condensates, whereas diphosphorylated PD-1 competitively binds the CD28 ICD and dissolves these assemblies. CD28 and PD-1 ICDs also undergo condensation directly, revealing a dynamic and compositionally heterogeneous signaling system. Guided by this competitive condensation mechanism, we engineer CD28 ICD mutants that preserve Lck condensation while resisting PD-1-mediated disruption. Incorporation of these condensation-selective mutants into Chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) constructs confers resistance to inhibitory signaling and enhances antitumor efficacy in vivo. These findings establish condensation as a central organizing principle of CD28 costimulation and provide a biophysical framework for…

items.title: Random, fragile, or correlated: Mechanisms of synteny decay in mammals
items.summary_raw: We formalize three models of genome evolution, yielding analytical distributions of synteny block sizes between pairs of genomes. To evaluate each model, we fit theoretical synteny block size distributions to empirical distributions from a comparative analysis of nearly 200 mammalian genomes. Between the random breakage model (RBM), with uniformly distributed breakpoints, the fragile breakage model (FBM) with breakpoint hotspots, and what we term the correlated breakage model (CBM) with pairs of nearby breakpoints, we find that the FBM and CBM are far more consistent with mammalian genome evolution than the RBM. Inferred parameters of each model qualitatively agree with previously calculated rates of mammalian genome evolution. The FBM and CBM perform comparably with each other, suggesting that either model could serve as an improved null model of genome evolution to use in statistical tests for syntenic regions that are unlikely to exist due to random chance.

items.title: Linguistic intervention unlocks the economic gains of diversity
items.summary_raw: Gains from trade generate prosperity, yet interpersonal exchange can falter along racial lines. We study incentivized experimental economies where participants must spontaneously initiate and sustain trading relationships with others whose race is visible. When the highest gains from trade require cross-race exchange, diverse economies underperform: welfare and specialization suffer as many retreat to autarky. This underperformance reflects not segregation into racial trading blocs, but a collapse in exchange. Opportunities for contact alone do not close the performance gap, which persists and even widens over time. To understand why, we turn to communication itself. Lower welfare is associated with less communication, fewer expressions of affiliation and achievement, and less explicit signaling of needs, deficits, and surpluses. We call this communicative misalignment: differences in shared-language use that raise search, bargaining, and coordination costs. A brief linguistic intervention equips participants with a communicative toolkit. It increases communication volume and the frequency of motivational and state-signaling language. Crucially, when gains depend on cross-race exchange, the intervention restores specialization and cross-race trade, closing the performance gap. Its effects are minimal when efficient trade need not cross race, indicating specificity rather than generic skill training. Language thus operates bidirectionally, both revealing the state of…

items.title: Mass-independent oxygen isotope fractionation driven by energetic-particle irradiation of icy solids
items.summary_raw: Mass-independent isotope fractionation (MIF) of oxygen provides key insights into atmospheric chemistry and the origin of isotopic anomalies in planetary materials. To date, MIF has been primarily associated with gas-phase processes involving symmetry-dependent reaction pathways, most notably ozone formation. Whether analogous effects can arise in condensed phases or at interfaces remains an open question. Here we report laboratory experiments demonstrating that energetic particle irradiation of icy oxide surfaces produces mass-independent oxygen isotope fractionation at temperatures as low as 10 K. Electron irradiation of SiO 2 and Al 2 O 3 substrates in the presence of H 2 O ice results in measurable shifts in Δ 17 O in the underlying solids. The resulting three-isotope relationships include slope-1-like behavior in SiO 2 and Al 2 O 3 and distinct, substrate-dependent trends in Al 2 O 3 , indicating that irradiation-induced defect formation and interfacial chemistry govern the isotope effects. The magnitude of the observed anomalies demonstrates that irradiation-driven processes can generate substantial oxygen isotope heterogeneity in condensed phases. These results identify a previously unrecognized class of MIF and provide a quantitative framework for interpreting oxygen isotope signatures in radiation-processed environments, including interstellar grains and early solar system materials.

items.title: Correction for Liu et al., A spinoreticular pathway mediates nocifensive responses to noxious mechanical stimuli
IL36γ signaling promotes mammalian anti-tick immunity
items.summary_raw: Ticks, like Ixodes scapularis , can parasitize a diverse array of vertebrates, favoring natural hosts but feeding opportunistically on others. Natural hosts, as well as permissive hosts such as laboratory mice, tolerate repeated infestations, while many incidental hosts may acquire anti-tick immunity, as first described in guinea pigs. We show that tick-immune guinea pigs display altered dermal cytology and a distinct transcriptome, predominantly upregulating the IL36γ cytokine. Interference with IL36γ signaling, via gene knockdown, chemical inhibition, or its natural antagonist IL36RN, reversed anti-tick immunity in guinea pigs. Conversely, genome engineering to silence IL36RN in C3H mice, representing a permissive host, disrupted tick engorgement, interfering with the transmission of Lyme disease pathogens. These findings firmly establish IL36γ as a central mediator of protective anti-tick immunity involving I. scapularis in mammalian hosts and support future strategies to interfere with tick-transmitted infections.

THE TOP FIVE 1. We’re already feeling 1.5 degrees Celsius. Now we’re locking it in. El Niño is giving us a taste of what the warming we have locked in as a species will feel like. Just look at the extreme weather that raged this summer in the form of storms and heat waves as the cyclical weather pattern drove up temperature averages past 1.5 degrees Celsius above pre-industrial levels. That’s the maximum warming benchmark set in the 2015 Paris Agreement, later reinforced in a landmark 2018 United Nations report. Now the latest data from the UN Environment Programme shows that we’re well on our way to making this year’s El Niño the new norm. A report released Wednesday suggests the current trajectory of emissions means the “lowest possible” warming scenario would lead to global temperatures peaking at about 1.7 degrees to 1.8 degrees by midcentury before potentially returning to 1.5 degrees by 2100. To put the world on that pathway, global emissions would need to fall by 18% in the next three years relative to 2025 levels. Then 45% by 2035. Then another 69% by 2040. The world is a long way…

items.title: Geothermal Insiders Unpack the Fervo Short
items.summary_raw: Few startups have as much riding on their success as Fervo Energy. To many concerned about climate change, the company, which taps underground heat to generate electricity, represents a source of hope for a clean energy future because it promises to produce carbon-free power around the clock, unlike wind and solar. Now that Fervo has gone public , however, it’s opened itself up to new scrutiny about whether it can deliver on its promise. In early October, a short seller called Morpheus Research published what it presented as blockbuster findings that Fervo was “unraveling” and that its first commercial project was “destined for failure.” The report alleged that Fervo struggled with declining temperatures at its pilot project and is facing water loss issues and trouble accessing transmission at its first commercial plant. Fervo’s stock, which debuted at $27 per share, was already down to $14.33 prior to the report’s publication after rising interest rates drove a broader market pullback from clean energy stocks. The market also appeared to react after the company told investors in August that its transmission partners “are managing unique circumstances in 2027 that may result in Fervo being curtailed for a period of time.” Since the Morpheus report came out, the stock has sunk another 30%. items.title: Town leaders chided residents for warning of flash floods. Then, the river took two children.
items.summary_raw: Peak tourist season had arrived in Ruidoso, New Mexico, and Mayor Lynn Crawford was campaigning to convince the public that the village was safe. A Republican with white hair and a Texas drawl, Crawford said he was frustrated with residents who were sharing warnings of flooding on social media. “They spout stuff off,” he said in a radio address on June 30, 2025. “And I don’t know why they’re so afraid. I do not understand it.” The community had experienced severe flooding the previous summer, after two wildfires burned 25,000 acres above town, in the Sacramento Mountains. The fires and floods had destroyed about 1,000 homes. Together, the Village of Ruidoso and its smaller neighbor, Ruidoso Downs, are home to some 10,000 residents, but that number more than doubles during the summer. Since then, residents had been on edge. A new monsoon season had arrived, bringing sporadic flooding that jeopardized the town’s economic engine of horse racing. At stake were big crowds to celebrate the Fourth of July, watch quarter horse racing, and enjoy cool weather that’d lured Texans here for generations. “We have flooding temporarily,” Crawford had told a Texas news anchor in an interview. “And just almost as fast as it came to town, and went through town, it’s gone.” Crawford, who is 64, managed an exclusive club at the Ruidoso Downs Race Track & Casino and once called that his “real job.” He made less than $26,000 as mayor. But if the town’s economy was precarious, so was its geography…

items.title: At the Wall of Wind, engineers blow homes apart to learn how to save them

Then the 12 massive fans arrayed across the 14-foot-high Wall of Wind accelerate in unison, forcing air across the laboratory at highway speeds. The manufactured home begins to shudder on its supports. A roar fills the testing facility. The engineers keep cranking up the fans. Hundreds of pressure sensors dot the structure, but some of what the researchers are learning in this laboratory at Florida International University can be seen with the naked eye. As the wind pushes against the walls and over the roof, a window blows out. The house strains against the steel straps and anchors holding it down. They begin to snap. The last three break in unison. The entire structure pitches back, then overturns. That is exactly what Elaina Sutley wants to see. items.title: In Michigan, 3 tribes are on a mission to bring back a fish that disappeared 100 years ago
items.summary_raw: Even when they’re young, the characteristic iridescent hues of the Arctic grayling are noticeable at the right angle. On a brisk morning in September, fish and wildlife biologist Sean Leask counted and measured hundreds of these fish, which were raised at the Grand Traverse Band of Ottawa and Chippewa Indians’ streamside rearing facility, located just outside Traverse City in northern Michigan. “Some of these might be catchable by the end of next year,” Leask said. “I don’t know what their growth will look like in the wild.” That’s because Arctic grayling haven’t been seen in Michigan waters for almost a century. By the 1930s, industrial activity like logging and overfishing, along with competition from non-native fish, had decimated their numbers. But three northern Michigan tribes and the state are trying to change that by reintroducing the fish to local waters. “Our taking care of them and helping them to reestablish their population helps us to reestablish ourselves, our culture, and our traditions,” said Tina Frankenberger, the Grand Traverse Band’s tribal environmental resiliency lead. Their work joins broader efforts by tribes around the country to restore native species — from salmon to oysters to condors — that are culturally and economically important, while also strengthening the ecosystems that these species depend on against threats like climate change. items.title: Does the climate-adaptive city pilot policy exacerbate urban sprawl? Evidence from a quasi-natural experiment in China
Climate crisis and livable futures: Ursula K. Le Guin’s utopias and solarpunk fiction
items.summary_raw: While literary responses to global environmental change have been varied, many have adopted a dystopian tone offering bleak visions of the future and thus helping to reinforce present-day perspectives and prevent action. In this essay, I examine texts that diverge from the prevailing apocalyptic mode and propose a more optimistic vision of the future: neither narratives of catastrophe and extinction nor eco-modernist tales of techno-optimism, these – what I call – ‘modest utopias’ sketch scenarios of livable futures beyond the Anthropocene. I discuss Ursula K. Le Guin’s work as an important model for this way of writing and thinking about the future and climate change, focusing in particular on her Always coming home (1985) and some selected essays. Novels, as Le Guin claimed in “The carrier bag theory of fiction,” are best seen as medicine bundles “holding things in a particular, powerful relation to one another and to us” (2019b: 933). Accordingly, my exploration of Le Guin’s works traces the relations they have helped establish in contemporary critical theory and climate fiction and examines the latter’s efforts to transform the present by imagining habitable futures through solarpunk utopias that are participatory, peaceful, and nurturing, and that focus on process and relations rather than on progress and growth.

items.title: Climate change and conflict: The vicious cycles undermining climate action, and what can be done to break them
items.summary_raw: Abstract In this review, we synthesize evidence to argue that climate change and conflict are mutually reinforcing. We first examine conflict as a barrier to mitigation, focusing on four faultlines that slow climate action: (a) ideological polarization, (b) “elite versus ordinary people” narratives, (c) intranational, place‐based conflicts, and (d) international disputes. The consequence of these conflicts is worsening climate change, which in turn increases the prevalence of factors known to be conflict amplifiers: heat stress, economic stress, widening inequality, and forced displacement. Our analysis points to the potential for recursive “climate–conflict loops”, fuelled in part by erosion of institutional trust, shrinking moral circles, political polarization, and de‐prioritization of long‐term climate goals. In a spirit of optimism, however, we identify three buffers capable of breaking these vicious cycles: maintenance of procedural and distributive justice, enhancing information integrity, and scaffolding institutional cooperation. We conclude by proposing a research agenda that integrates psychological mechanisms into dynamic, multi‐level accounts of how climate impacts and political conflict coevolve.

items.title: Climate change and relational landscapes in the Arctic: intergenerational perspectives from Tuktoyaktuk, Canada
items.summary_raw: Abstract Across the Arctic, rapid and unprecedented climate change is reshaping ecosystems and human systems alike, impacting the conditions that support health and well-being, known as the social determinants of health. Guided by holistic understandings of health and a strength-based approach, this research aims to document community-level conditions in the Inuvialuit Hamlet of Tuktoyaktuk that support sense of place, health, and well-being across generations, and describe how and where these conditions are influenced by climate-driven landscape changes. Findings draw on data collected using photovoice with 6 high school youth and semi-structured interviews with 21 adults and Elders. Results highlight that climate drivers of change are impacting the different facets of health—mental, physical, and relational—as well as the conditions that sustain them. Across age groups, participants emphasized that relationships with each other, with Inuvialuit culture, and with place are central to being healthy and well. These relationships are nurtured both within the community and through time spent out on the land. Prioritizing locally identified needs and intergenerational perspectives within climate change research and adaptation can guide context-specific strategies that centre the health of people and of the land. Grounding adaptation in this way moves beyond physical protections against natural hazards to sustaining the social and cultural ties embedded in place, thereby…

items.title: Design of Photovoltaic Applications in the Built Environment: A Critical Review
items.summary_raw: Photovoltaic (PV) technology has made significant progress since the International Energy Agency (IEA) proposed the concept of PV application in the built environment in 1997. This paper reviews PV applications in the built environment across three phases: pre-design, design, and post-design. A PRISMA-informed search was conducted in Web of Science Core Collection and Scopus, covering publications from January 2005 to August 2026. After screening, 211 publications were included in the review, and 238 references were cited in total, including 27 pre-2005 background sources. In the pre-design phase, the scopes and impacts of PV application in the built environment are reviewed. In the design phase, design strategies are examined in terms of PV module selection, mounting configuration, array layout, and geometric design parameters. In the post-design phase, power potential, economic potential, aesthetic environment, and safety reporting are reviewed. Based on these findings, a consultative and iterative design workflow is proposed. It integrates stakeholder priorities, multi-scale spatial data, climate-specific economic parameters, and construct-specific aesthetic and social evaluation. However, the workflow is conceptual and has not yet been empirically validated. Its potential to improve public acceptance and facilitate implementation therefore requires future testing in real projects. The review provides a structured reference for urban planners, architects, and developers…

items.title: Robust Coordinated Reserve Optimization Method for Electricity–Gas Systems Considering Multi‐Source Coupling and Multiple Uncertainties
items.summary_raw: ABSTRACT To address operational uncertainties in integrated energy systems (IES) while considering renewable energy utilization and carbon emissions, a two‐stage robust reserve scheduling model is proposed for existing electricity–gas systems. The model accounts for wind and photovoltaic power fluctuations and transmission‐line N − 1 contingencies, while incorporating a tiered carbon emission cost into day‐ahead scheduling. Electricity and gas reserves are jointly allocated in the day‐ahead stage and coordinated during intraday adjustment to balance operating costs, renewable curtailment, and load‐shedding risks. First‐order Taylor linearization, strong duality, and a Big‐M formulation are applied to reformulate the intraday subproblem, and the model is solved using a column‐and‐constraint generation algorithm. Case studies on a coupled electricity–gas test system indicate that coordinated reserve scheduling promotes wind and solar utilization, and alleviates load‐shedding risks under multiple uncertainties. Incorporation of carbon emission costs encourages lower emission dispatch, with corresponding changes in operating costs and reserve allocation. These findings reveal the trade‐offs among operational robustness, economic performance, and emission reduction, demonstrating the potential of coordinated electricity–gas reserves to support renewable energy integration and low‐carbon operation.

items.title: Scaling climate adaptation planning: impacts and limitations of California’s Senate Bill 379 for local planning
items.summary_raw: Abstract This study examines the impact of the first state-level climate change adaptation planning mandate in the United States, California’s Senate Bill 379 (SB379). We analyze the content of local plans before and after the mandate and compare the quality of the mandated plans with a sample of voluntary climate change adaptation plans developed by local governments across the U.S. The research finds that plans developed after the mandate incorporated more climate adaptation strategies, a greater variety of strategy types, and addressed a wider range of climate hazards. The mandate is associated with increased “mainstreaming” of climate adaptation, primarily through add-on and programmatic strategies. SB379-mandated plans scored higher overall compared to voluntary climate plans from other states but lower on addressing uncertainty. The findings indicate that state mandates like SB379 can effectively catalyze local climate adaptation planning, but challenges remain in achieving high-quality, actionable plans across diverse communities.

items.title: Carbon sequestration strategies for climate resilience: Sorghum‐based innovations for sustainable agriculture in dryland regions
items.summary_raw: Societal Impact Statement Climate change is intensifying heat, drought, and food insecurity, threatening dryland farming and carbon management worldwide. We reviewed research on sorghum, a drought‐adapted C4 crop, covering physiology, roots, biomass allocation, soil carbon, bioenergy, breeding, phenotyping, management, and policy. Sorghum can sustain production under water‐limited conditions and may support durable soil‐carbon storage via deep roots, residues, mycorrhizal pathways, and conservation practices, though long‐term validation is needed. These findings underscore sorghum's value for sustainable, climate‐resilient agriculture, and the urgent need for carbon‐aware breeding, farmer‐centered adoption, improved residue management, and credible, affordable, and accessible carbon accounting for farmers and policymakers in drylands globally. Summary Sorghum ( Sorghum bicolor L. Moench), a hardy C4 crop, uniquely addresses the dual challenges of rising atmospheric CO 2 and global food security. Its high biomass production, deep roots, and drought tolerance make it ideal for dryland farming. This review explores how sorghum captures atmospheric CO 2 , distributes it within the plant, and adds to soil carbon stores. It emphasizes processes such as photosynthesis efficiency, biomass allocation, and residue breakdown, which are affected by soil microbes and sorghum's residue chemistry. The review also explores the balance between grain yield and carbon storage, highlighting how…

items.title: EFL Students’ Responses to English-Language Climate Change Discourse: An Ecolinguistic and Local Wisdom Perspective
items.source_name: ALINEA Jurnal Bahasa Sastra dan Pengajarannya
items.summary_raw: English-language climate change discourse shapes how readers understand the ecological crisis, yet little is known about how English as a Foreign Language (EFL) students in non-Western contexts respond to it. This study examined Bugis-Makassar EFL students’ responses to this discourse, focusing on the ecolinguistic features of their writing, their interpretation of the texts, and the local wisdom they draw on. Using a qualitative descriptive design, the study analyzed written reflections from 20 English Literature students at Universitas Hasanuddin who read three genres of climate texts: an IPCC report, a COP30 decision, and a BBC news articles. Reflections were analyzed using Stibbe’s ecological discourse analysis and transitivity and modality analysis based on Systemic Functional Grammar, and triangulated with semi-structured interviews with 20 students. Material processes dominated the 82 ideational clauses analyzed (61.0%), but human agents were often replaced by abstractions or removed through passive constructions. Students built strong urgency through high modality and scientific and moral framing, while destructive metaphors were largely absorbed from the source texts. Thirteen reflections were beneficial, seven ambivalent, and none destructive; ambivalence arose from anthropocentrism. Local wisdom appeared spontaneously in only three reflections, through the Bugis rituals mappadendang and mappanini bosi, while one interviewee linked the COP30 term mutirão to gotong…

items.title: Workplace Mobbing and Employee Well-being: Associations with Burnout, Job Satisfaction, and Organizational Climate
items.summary_raw: Workplace mobbing is an important psychosocial occupational risk associated with adverse employee outcomes. This study examined associations between exposure to workplace mobbing, burnout symptoms, job satisfaction, selected psychosomatic symptoms, and perceived team atmosphere among 302 economically active adults from the Silesian Voivodeship, Poland. Data were collected between October 2025 and January 2026 using an anonymous original 29-item questionnaire. Fisher’s exact test, the Mann–Whitney U test, and Spearman’s rank correlation were used. Mobbing experience was reported by 58.3% of respondents. Burnout symptoms were more frequent among respondents reporting public humiliation and criticism (55.8% vs. 17.2%; p < 0.001). Participants reporting mobbing consistently showed lower job satisfaction across all analysed dimensions (all p < 0.001). No statistically significant associations were found between mobbing experience and gender, age, or length of employment. Supervisors’ effective responses to mobbing were strongly positively correlated with perceived team atmosphere (rho = 0.61; p < 0.001). The findings highlight the organizational consequences of workplace mobbing and the importance of effective managerial responses.

Caring, sharing and mobilizing – information sharing practices among Swedish climate activists
items.summary_raw: Purpose The study investigates how participants in the Swedish climate grassroot activist group Rebellmammorna engage in information sharing practices related to climate change. Design/methodology/approach The study uses 10 semi-structured interviews with participants in the Swedish grassroot climate activist group Rebellmammorna. It is informed by New Feminist Materialist Science and Technology studies and draws on Puig de la Bellacasa’s concept of care. Maternal identity, rituals and storytelling are used as analytical concepts. Findings This study of Rebellmammorna shows climate activists’ engagement with information as a form of care work rooted in the desire to protect their children and securing livable futures for them. Motherhood functions as a collective and strategic identity granting public authority, though creating vulnerabilities highlighting this legitimacy’s fragility. Care relations foster trust and sustain activism. Self-care enables continued engagement, while mutual care maintains group cohesion with fellow participants as trusted information sources. Shared stories and rituals enacting maternal identity mediate information exchange, strengthening community bonds and supporting broader public mobilization. Originality/value This study highlights how emotional, relational and embodied experiences shape the interpretation, evaluation, circulation and collective production of information within the grassroots climate activism of Rebellmammorna.
