From Puffery to Greenwashing: Vague Environmental and Climate-Related Claims under EU and UK Consumer Law
items.source_name: Lecture Notes in Education Psychology and Public Media
items.summary_raw: Environmental and climate-related claims increasingly occupy a contested boundary between lawful commercial puffery and actionable greenwashing. This paper examines how EU and UK consumer law determines when vague sustainability language becomes legally misleading. Through a comparative analysis of the EU Unfair Commercial Practices Directive, Directive (EU) 2024/825, the UK Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act 2024, relevant regulatory guidance, and selected decisions involving SHEIN, HSBC, Lufthansa, and KLM, the paper identifies three interrelated considerations: whether a claim conveys verifiable environmental implications, whether it creates a misleading overall impression through omission or selective framing, and whether it is capable of affecting the transactional decisions of the average consumer. It further distinguishes this general analysis from specific practices prohibited in all circumstances under the amended UCPD. The paper argues that substantiation requirements should correspond to the factual implications reasonably conveyed by an environmental claim, while preserving appropriate space for legitimate commercial promotion and expression.

items.title: Digital Transformation of Haryana Agriculture: Strengthening Climate Resilience and Advancing the Sustainable Development Goals
items.source_name: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
items.summary_raw: Climate change has surfaced as one of the most pivotal challenges confronting the agricultural sector, especially in agrarian regions vulnerable to resource degradation, water scarcity, and climate uncertainties. Haryana, a leading agricultural state in India, has faced significant environmental pressures in recent years, including declining groundwater levels, erratic rainfall patterns, rising temperatures, and soil degradation, necessitating the adoption of climate-resilient agricultural strategies. Against this backdrop, Information and Communication Technology has gained considerable importance as a transformative mechanism for strengthening agricultural sustainability, adaptive capacity, and informed decision-making among farmers. ICT-enabled interventions such as mobile-based advisory services, precision farming technologies, digital marketplaces, weather forecasting systems, remote sensing, and various e-governance platforms have increasingly contributed to improving agricultural efficiency and resilience. The present study aims to evaluate the role of ICT-enabled agricultural practices in Haryana and their contribution to climate resilience and to achieve the Sustainable Development Goals. This study applies a descriptive and analytical approach, drawing on secondary data and narrative review methodology. The study utilizes secondary data from government reports, policy documents, research articles, institutional publications, and international development reports on…

items.title: Framing the Future: Generational Populism in Youth-Led Climate Activism
items.summary_raw: Abstract The climate crisis is increasingly framed as an issue of intergenerational injustice, shaping how young people mobilize around the issue. This paper uses the concept of generational populism to examine how Fridays for Future (FFF) activists use populist generational discourse to mobilize around the climate crisis, using a mixed-methods text analysis of speeches by leading FFF activists that combines clause-based semantic text analysis and qualitative content analysis. The analysis reveals a strongly asymmetrical pattern: activists construct a decidedly generational populist ‘we’, while referring to the elite almost exclusively in conventional populist terms rather than generational ones. The activists tend to position themselves and the movement as active political subjects rather than passive victims. These findings identify a distinct variant of generational populism and highlight how generational populist framing can be used to construct an inclusive populist discourse centered on intergenerational justice.

items.title: Switching tracks: from resistance to acceptance in railway infrastructure projects
items.summary_raw: This study examines the determinants of public acceptance of railway infrastructure projects and the role of public participation in shaping such acceptance. The analysis is based on a Germany-wide survey of 2,632 respondents, combining a 2 × 3 factorial vignette experiment with hierarchical regression, structural equation modeling, and analysis of variance. The findings indicate that socio-psychological factors ( R 2 ≈ 84%) explain public acceptance substantially, with self-efficacy emerging as the central predictor through both direct and indirect effects via perceived risk. However, the cross-sectional relationships do not allow for causal conclusions. The role of public participation must be viewed in a nuanced way: the results show small but significant differences in perceived social justice across the experimental conditions, but no significant differences in public acceptance. Furthermore, compared to participation announced by the municipality, participation announced by the transport operator is associated with slightly higher trust in the operator and perceived risk. The results provide insights for designing participation processes in the German transport sector and shed light on the social aspects of sustainable infrastructure planning.

Fragile against what? Imagining climate change resilience by unmasking governance fragility
items.summary_raw: Since the 1990s, fragility has been used to describe low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) with limited ability to respond to external threats in ways that ensure citizen safety, security, and welfare. Fragility challenges us to engage with governance, including why and how many institutions (including those in high-income countries) fail to protect citizens during climate change. We ask the question: how can state fragility be applied, critiqued, and expanded when considering climate change, including anthropogenic drivers, extreme weather events, mitigation, and adaptation? We present a globally applicable framework of governance fragility and emphasise the role of institutional-level gaps in motivation/willingness to act, evidence uptake, and implementation in creating fragilities that inhibit climate resilience. Using the United States as a case study, we apply the framework to identify the political ideologies that inform institutional-level motivations, shape evidence uptake, and moderate implementation capacity. This expanded notion of governance fragility (beyond conflict-affected LMICs) offers a globally-relevant lens to imagine possible solutions, including a research-to-practice agenda that contends both with ideology/willingness to act and decentralised forms of climate governance in the face of national-level fragilities.

items.title: Associations of organisational climate and physical activity with attitudes toward sport and burnout among school administrators
items.summary_raw: Introduction School administrators operate under substantial stress associated with heavy workloads, increasing managerial responsibilities, and organisational pressures. These conditions may be associated with higher levels of burnout. This study examined the associations among school administrators’ perceptions of organisational climate, physical activity levels, attitudes toward sport, and occupational burnout, with particular attention to their public-health relevance. Methods The study included 223 school administrators from different school types. Data were collected using the Organisational Climate Scale, International Physical Activity Questionnaire-Short Form (IPAQ-SF), Attitudes Toward Sport Scale, and Burnout Scale. Associations among the variables were analysed using structural equation modelling (SEM). Physical activity was operationalised as the continuous total IPAQ-SF MET-min/week score derived from walking, moderate-intensity activity, and vigorous-intensity activity. Results Positive and statistically significant associations were observed between organisational climate and attitudes toward sport and between physical activity and attitudes toward sport. Organisational climate, physical activity, and attitudes toward sport were each significantly and negatively associated with occupational burnout. In the structural model, organisational climate and physical activity accounted for 34% of the variance in attitudes toward sport, whereas organisational climate…

items.title: Soil Salinity under Climate Change in Pakistan: Emerging Challenges and Sustainable Management Approaches for Agriculture
items.source_name: Kashmir Journal of Academic Research and Development
items.summary_raw: Soil salinity is a major constraint to agricultural productivity, soil health, and food security in Pakistan, particularly under changing climatic conditions. Rising temperatures, increased evapotranspiration, irregular precipitation, droughts, flooding, and sea-level rise can intensify salt accumulation and alter soil–water interactions. This review examines the emerging challenges associated with climate change and soil salinity in Pakistan, focusing on their impacts on soil properties, crop physiology, agricultural production, and rural livelihoods. It discusses the mechanisms of soil salinity and sodicity, their spatial distribution, and the interactions among climate variability, irrigation practices, groundwater quality, and secondary salinization. Furthermore, sustainable management approaches are evaluated, including gypsum application, organic amendments, integrated nutrient management, efficient irrigation, drainage improvement, and appropriate leaching strategies. Climate-resilient approaches, such as conventional crop breeding, modern biotechnology, halophyte utilization, plant growth-promoting microorganisms, and mycorrhizal associations, are also explored. The review highlights the potential of remote sensing, geographic information systems, precision agriculture, and predictive modelling to support salinity monitoring and site-specific management. Despite these opportunities, important challenges remain, including insufficient long-term monitoring, limited…

items.title: Simulation of errors related to the VLBI transmitter on Genesis and their impact on the terrestrial reference frame
items.summary_raw: Mission Genesis of the European Space Agency has been approved for launch in 2028. Its primary goal is the enhancement of the terrestrial reference frame by establishing a space tie on the Genesis satellite between all space geodetic techniques used for the determination of the frame. The satellite will be equipped with a dedicated Very Long Baseline Interferometry (VLBI) transmitter for geodesy. In this work, simulation studies with a global 20-station VLBI network are carried out to assess the impact of errors related to the VLBI transmitter on the terrestrial reference frame, more precisely on station coordinates derived from VLBI observations to Genesis. Our findings indicate that the calibration of the position of the VLBI transmitter on Genesis is critical for the success of the mission. Errors in the position at the one-centimeter-level will cause station coordinate errors of several millimeters. In particular, the tangential and cross-track components do have a significant influence. The precision of the VLBI group delays, however, is not as critical. Simulating white noise for the group delays of 40 ps does still yield station coordinate accuracies at the millimeter level, if estimated in a global solution from weekly 24-h sessions over five years. Considering the investigated aspects, the simulations confirm that the VLBI-related goals of Genesis can be achieved, if stringent requirements with the VLBI transmitter are fulfilled.

items.title: Increased southward swings of the South Indian convergence zone under greenhouse warming
items.summary_raw: Nature Climate Change, Published online: 20 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41558-026-02767-x Extreme southward swings of the South Indian convergence zone can lead to severe rainfall and flooding in southern Africa. Here the authors show that climate change leads to an increase in the frequency and intensity of such swings.

items.title: Incivility in Public Health Policy Discussions Spills Over to Public Engagement with Climate Issues: Evidence from English Language Social Media
items.summary_raw: Abstract Affective polarization and political sorting drive public antagonism around climate change and other issues at the science-policy nexus. We study cross-domain spillover of incivility in public engagements with climate change and public health on English language Twitter and Reddit using the COVID-19 period as a case study. To assess whether spillover exists between these two policy domains, we examined how the incivility of climate discussions on social media varied by their co-occurrence with COVID-19 content and temporal coincidence with pandemic events. We find strong evidence of the signatures of affective polarization surrounding COVID-19 spilling into the climate change domain. Across different social media systems, COVID-19 content is associated with incivility in climate discussions. These patterns of increased antagonism were responsive to pandemic events that made the link between science and public policy more salient. We also looked at how climate discussions about international organizations and elites changed with the pandemic's onset to show that the observed incivility spillover activated along overlapping pre-pandemic political cleavages, specifically anti-internationalist populist beliefs that linked climate policy opposition to vaccine hesitancy. Our findings show how affective polarization in public engagement with science becomes entrenched across policy domains, which has implications for how the public engages with and communicates about…

items.title: Targeting high-value uses to unlock the mitigation potential of clean hydrogen
items.summary_raw: Nature Climate Change, Published online: 20 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41558-026-02766-y Clean hydrogen is a versatile decarbonization option, but given its energy-intensive production, high costs and limited near-term supply, uses with the greatest environmental and economic benefits must be prioritized. Analysis of ten end-use sectors identifies high-value applications and suggests that uniform supply-side subsidies risk misallocating clean hydrogen and public funds, highlighting the need for sector-specific demand-side policies.

items.title: Historical trends show more declining than increasing species among European pollinators
items.summary_raw: Anthropogenic global change presents a growing threat to insect pollinators. Yet, long-term, continental-scale assessments of their population trends remain limited. Here, we leveraged a curated database of over four million occurrence records, covering 88% of extant bee and hoverfly species in Europe, to assess persistence, richness, and occupancy trends over the past century. Species persistence at the European level was relatively high, with modern records available for 87% of bee and 89% of hoverfly species. Regional richness changes were modest, with declines in the Atlantic and Continental regions for both pollinator groups. Recent increases were observed in the Alpine region for bees, but species richness remained largely stable elsewhere. At the species level, however, a more concerning picture emerged: Most bee species and about half of hoverfly species declined in occupancy. Species traits explained little variation in these trends, although there was a weak tendency for cold-adapted bees to show steeper declines than warm-adapted ones. Genera showing some of the steepest declines include parasitic or dietary specialists, though neither of these traits significantly predicted occupancy trends. Overall, we highlight clear warning signs of species population declines, but with potential recovery opportunities if we take urgent actions to reverse those trends.

items.title: Correction for Matt et al., An aquaglyceroporin governs cellular water and CO 2 conductance relevant for vesicular mineral formation in a marine calcifier
Immense but not immutable: A sudden and sustained decline in deep-pelagic life in a large oceanic ecosystem
items.summary_raw: The deep-pelagic habitat of the Gulf of Mexico comprises 90.4% of its volume and houses an exceptionally diverse deep-pelagic animal community that provides numerous ecosystem services, including carbon cycling and prey provisioning for oceanic predators. Here, we report sudden, severe, and persistent declines in the abundance of deep-pelagic fishes, crustaceans, and cephalopods that have persisted for over a decade. Over a 3.5-y period, animal abundances declined by 60 to 85%, taxon depending. Particularly hard-hit were ecologically foundational taxa such as euphausiids and lanternfishes. The magnitude of population-level decline that occurred during this 3.5-y period was greater than any observed over a 60-y period in the California Current system, the only comparable dataset, making this the fastest and most severe faunal decline reported for Earth’s largest ecosystem type. These declines were detected both via direct sampling and acoustic sensing, providing independent corroboration. Genomic analyses indicate reductions in genetic diversity among dominant taxa, both a corroboration and a consequence of the decline. Furthermore, resource managers report that these trends parallel those of managed or protected Gulf species that are dependent on deep-pelagic prey, including endangered species (e.g., beaked whales, Rice’s whale). No naturally occurring factors (e.g., temperature, oxygen, food supply) correlated with the observed declines, suggesting an anthropogenic…

items.title: Catalytic reactive-hydrogen membranes for rapid capture and hydrodefluorination of six PFAS of regulatory concern
items.summary_raw: Per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) persist in aquatic environments due to their ultrastable C–F bonds and poor susceptibility to conventional treatment. Here, we report an H 2 -based catalytic-film membrane that enables PFAS destruction in ambient conditions by generating highly reactive surface (H ads * ) and subsurface hydrogen (H sub * ), the latter stored as β-phase palladium hydride (β-PdHx). Solid-state analyses evidenced β-PdHx formation and related lattice expansion with elevated H 2 chemical potential, revealing a structural mechanism that links hydrogen storage to catalytic defluorination. Mechanistically, the two hydrogen species play complementary roles: H ads * -rich Pd 0 surface enabled PFAS capture through parallel adsorption to maximize interfacial contact with active H, whereas sustained H sub * supplied the energetic driving force for stepwise hydrodefluorination consistent with sequential C–F scission. As a result, across six PFAS of regulatory concern—PFOA, PFOS, PFNA, PFHxS, PFBS, and GenX—the catalytic membrane converted all contaminants toward fully defluorinated products. Long-chain PFAS were removed and defluorinated more rapidly than short-chain analogs, while GenX showed greater recalcitrance due to its ether linkage, weaker adsorption, and higher average C–F bond dissociation energy; nonetheless, GenX still exhibited removal and defluorination, with the production of 2-propoxypropanoic acid. The system also enabled continuous coremoval of…

items.title: Understory diversity is positively associated with overstory carbon sequestration
items.summary_raw: Forests are a major terrestrial carbon sink, and higher overstory diversity is often associated with greater carbon accrual in trees and soils. Yet the contribution of the understory vegetation, the most species-rich forest stratum, to tree and soil carbon accumulation remains largely unknown. Here, we analyzed Canada’s National Forest Inventory database to explore whether understory diversity (richness and evenness of shrubs, herbs, and bryophytes) is associated with carbon accumulation in overstory trees and soils across environmental gradients of air temperature, climate moisture, and nitrogen deposition. We found that herb and bryophyte species richness were positively associated with decadal tree carbon accumulation, with the strongest effects at warmer, drier, and nitrogen-limited sites. In contrast, understory diversity showed no consistent association with soil carbon accumulation. On a decadal scale, increasing herb and bryophyte species richness from their minimum to median values corresponded to 15% and 6% increases in tree carbon accumulation, respectively. These results provide large-scale observational evidence that diversity in lower vegetation layers is positively associated with overstory carbon sequestration and reveal strong environmental modulation of these multistratal biodiversity–ecosystem functioning relationships. These findings suggest that species-rich herb and bryophyte communities should be considered in strategies for sustaining forest carbon…

items.title: Neuromodulatory control of cortical function: Cell-type-specific regulation of neuronal information transfer
items.summary_raw: Neuromodulatory systems such as dopamine and acetylcholine enable cortical circuits to rapidly shift between behavioral states, yet it remains unclear how receptor-specific signaling reshapes what single neurons compute. Here, we combined whole-cell recordings from excitatory and inhibitory neurons in layer 2/3 of mouse somatosensory cortex with information-theoretic analyses under frozen-noise stimulation. We quantified stimulus-to-spike information transfer and profiled each neuron across four functional domains: passive membrane biophysics, action potential dynamics, intrinsic adaptation currents, and input feature selectivity captured by spike-triggered averages. Activation of D1, D2, or M1 receptors revealed three main findings. First, neuromodulators altered fractional information and firing output in a cell-type- and receptor-specific manner, demonstrating selective regulation of encoding. Second, unsupervised clustering based on functional attribute sets showed that receptor activation reorganizes baseline functional grouping, consistent with a dynamic computational phenotype. Third, multiset correlation and factor analysis revealed that neuromodulation systematically reorganizes covariance among functional domains. In excitatory neurons, dopaminergic activation decreased coordination between input feature selectivity and other functional properties while strengthening coordination among response-based features such as spike dynamics and adaptation. Inhibitory…

items.title: Biotic response networks are an important organizer of the transcriptome in wild Arabidopsis thaliana populations
items.summary_raw: Extensive laboratory experimentation has revealed conserved molecular pathways controlling growth and stress responses in plants, yet how these programs operate in natural settings remains poorly understood. We have investigated the organization of the transcriptome in wild populations of Arabidopsis thaliana by sampling plants across 60 natural sites in Europe and North America over two seasons. Transcriptomes varied extensively among individuals and were only weakly structured by geography or season. No groups of plants stood out due to clear biotic or abiotic stress signatures known from the laboratory. While only a small portion of transcriptome variance was explained by disease symptoms or environmental and phenotypic variables, infection-associated signals accounted for the largest share of the explainable fraction. Biotic-response networks identified in controlled laboratory conditions were well conserved in wild transcriptomes, while other networks, including abiotic-response networks were substantially reorganized in wild plants. Together, these results indicate that while certain transcriptional modules are easily reidentified when moving from the wild to controlled conditions, many regulatory relationships differ in these two contexts, highlighting how ecological complexity shapes transcriptome organization in natural populations.

items.title: Biodiversity supports coastal nutrient cycling with a stable source of fish excretion
Leveraging existing grid infrastructure for rapid US renewable and storage deployment
items.summary_raw: Rapid electricity demand growth, grid connection delays, and supply chain constraints create a serious risk of supply shortages and rising electricity costs in the next few years. This paper studies the strategy of adding colocated renewables and storage at existing power plants to take advantage of spare grid capacity. Using satellite imagery, we assess solar and wind potential near 3,890 U.S. fossil and renewable plants. By 2030, we find that existing fossil plants could host up to 597 GW of economically viable solar and wind without exceeding the existing interconnection capacity of each site. Existing renewable plants could host an additional 260 GW of firm capacity—comprising storage paired with added solar and wind capacity. These additions could accelerate clean energy deployment and enhance reliability and affordability, but realizing this potential is contingent upon regulatory reforms and coordinating the operational constraints of colocated resources.

items.title: mechanoLight: A genetically encoded fluorescent biosensor for visualizing 5-HT2AR mechanotransduction in live cells
items.summary_raw: G protein–coupled receptors (GPCRs) are pivotal sensors of the mechanical environment, yet how they sense and transduce physical stimuli into biochemical signals within live cells remains largely elusive. Here we introduce mechanoLight, a genetically encoded red fluorescent biosensor designed to report the mechanical activation of the 5-hydroxytryptamine 2A receptor (5-HT2AR). By incorporating a circularly permuted mApple (cp-mApple) into the third intracellular loop of 5-HT2AR with the optimized linker (m-linker), mechanoLight selectively detects conformational changes of 5-HT2AR in response to fluid shear stress while exhibiting minimal sensitivity to 5-HT. In sharp contrast, psychLight2, the previously developed green 5-HT2AR biosensor, primarily detects ligand-induced 5-HT2AR activation, suggesting that mechanoLight and psychLight2 capture distinct conformational modes of 5-HT2AR activation. Integrated analysis of linker-swapping experiments, structural modeling, and molecular dynamics simulations revealed that the flexibility of the m-linker underlies the mechanosensitivity of mechanoLight. We further extend this strategy to other mechanosensitive GPCRs, enabling visualization of their mechanoreactivity in live cells. The mechanoLight signal reflects the mechanosensitivity of 5-HT2AR, as shear stress-induced 5-HT2AR activation triggers Gα q -dependent signaling pathways, including phospholipase C (PLC) activation, intracellular Ca 2+ mobilization, and ERK…

items.title: Modeling the global potential of smart farming innovations
items.summary_raw: Smart farming innovations can improve agricultural productivity, resilience, and environmental sustainability, yet their real-world impact hinges on their diffusion dynamics, which in turn depend on their economic viability. We present here a global assessment of the profitability of smart farming innovation across croplands at a spatial resolution of ~5 km from the farmers’ and the societal perspectives. We cover application mapping for precision agriculture, automated application of inputs, autonomous weeding machines, GPS steering assistance systems, and autonomous irrigation systems. For this, we compiled a globally comprehensive dataset of smart farming innovation adoption locations (N = 4,422) based on a combination of a survey (N = 2,677) and a meta-analysis (N = 1,745) and combined them with remotely sensed and statistical data to train an ensemble of five geospatial machine learning models (generalized linear models, random forests, support vector machines, maximum entropy, and boosted regression trees), which show the global distribution of the different innovations’ profitability and its overlap with major environmental issues the innovations can help to mitigate. Simulations of future socioeconomic pathways combined with assumptions about future agri-environmental policies reveal that, especially in middle-income countries, the potential of smart farming will grow over time.

items.title: Toward cooler cities by larger homogeneous functional clusters
items.summary_raw: Urban heat island (UHI) intensifies heat-related risks and environmental degradation in cities worldwide, yet existing mitigation strategies have largely overlooked how the spatial scale of homogeneous functional building clusters influences local climate. This scale may matter because buildings with similar functions often share similar morphology, activity schedules, and anthropogenic heat-release patterns, allowing their spatial contiguity to shape ventilation and heat accumulation. Here, we introduce the Urban Homogeneous Scale (UHS)—an indicator that measures the spatial scale of contiguous, functionally similar building clusters—and analyze 233,844 observations across 101 global cities to assess its potential for mitigating surface UHI. We find that larger UHS is associated with lower surface UHI: every 100-meter increase in UHS corresponds to 4.5% decrease in daytime UHI. This daytime cooling effect is particularly more pronounced in inland, humid, and high-income regions. In low-income regions, larger building area and higher building volume more strongly weaken UHS cooling capacity than in wealthier regions, revealing a socioeconomic inequality in UHS’s mitigation benefits. Our findings identify the spatial scale of building clusters as a essential dimension of urban form associated with urban heat burden, and suggest that considering UHS alongside targeted controls on built environmental characteristics may inform future heat-mitigation planning.

items.title: Scientists disrupt less but more persistently with career aging
items.summary_raw: Disruption describes the extent to which a scientific work overturns the prior knowledge on which it builds and leads to a new line of research. A scientist’s tendency to produce disruptive work has been found recently to decline over the career. However, the disruption index captures only how strongly a paper overturns prior work and ignores whether that disruption is later accepted or overturned by subsequent research. The persistent disruption (PD) framework adds this second perspective, identifying work that disrupts prior research and is then consolidated rather than displaced by later work. We examine how PD evolves over the career and find the opposite pattern: The probability of producing a persistent disruptive paper increases with career age. Senior scientists disrupt prior work less often compared to young, but once they do, the disruption tends to persist rather than being quickly superseded. Our results suggest that this reversal feature is due to the experience and we corroborate it across several dimensions of recognition. We also show that, at a fixed level of disruptiveness, the more senior the scientist is, it attracts more citations, social-media attention, and research grants. Nobel laureates also show delayed persistent disruptions. They exhibit high disruptive ability early in their careers, yet their prize-winning work appears years later. This lag further indicates that experience is needed to turn disruptive ability into the field’s most celebrated…

A Bering Sea marine heatwave triggers unprecedented crab hybridization, challenging fisheries management
items.summary_raw: Marine heatwaves are increasingly recognized for their capacity to generate ecological surprises, yet the pathways that propagate these unexpected responses are often poorly understood. Here, we document an unanticipated ecological response 7 y after a Bering Sea marine heatwave, in which formerly rare snow crab ( Chionoecetes opilio ) × Tanner crab ( C. bairdi ) hybrid abundance increased 13.4-fold, and the proportion of commercial-sized hybrid males increased 13.1-fold, relative to historical averages. Using causal modeling, we show that the hybrid crab surge was mediated by a heatwave-induced collapse of snow crab rather than direct thermal effects on hybrid survival or increased spatial overlap between mature snow and Tanner crab. Our results reveal an indirect cascading pathway through which an extreme climate event triggered unexpected ecological consequences and unforeseen challenges for fisheries management in the Bering Sea. The dramatic increase in abundance of harvestable hybrid crab, coupled with their exclusion from existing management frameworks, highlights the vulnerability of inflexible management systems to unanticipated ecosystem responses.

items.title: Calibration, accuracy, and domain variation across one million collective forecasts from prediction platforms
items.summary_raw: Using approximately one million resolved contracts and questions across four collective forecasting platforms, twelve domains, and time horizons ranging from hours to years, we evaluate the calibration and accuracy of collective forecasts in real-world settings. We found that forecast probabilities were overall highly calibrated: events assigned a probability of p % occurred approximately p % of the time. This broad pattern was evident across platforms and many domains, although fine-grained analyses revealed systematic tendencies toward over- or underestimation in highly consequential areas. While this does not mean that forecasting platforms provide certainty about individual events, our findings suggest that large-scale aggregation of judgments contains meaningful information about real-world uncertainty; when examined in aggregate, the predictions generated by the platforms provided informative estimates of event likelihood.

items.title: Geography of groundwater use and depletion in internationally shared aquifers
items.summary_raw: Transboundary aquifers (TBAs) underlie 35% of global groundwater-irrigated cropland, yet few are covered by formal cooperative arrangements. Whether this limited cooperation is consequential depends in part on where groundwater is used within shared aquifers, because pumping far from international borders may generate little cross-border impact. Combining ∼ 116,000 well observations with global irrigation data across all 426 known TBAs, we assess how groundwater use and depletion differ from comparable domestic systems and how they are distributed relative to international borders. While we find no evidence of greater average depletion in TBAs, depletion is more strongly concentrated toward international borders in shared aquifers and varies substantially across systems. Irrigation is also more intensive and concentrated toward borders in shared aquifers, although much of this pattern is attenuated after accounting for border rivers. Groundwater-supplied irrigation remains more border-proximate after accounting for these rivers. A dyad-level typology distinguishes shared systems according to where groundwater demand is concentrated, linking their potential for cross-border interaction to different management options. These findings suggest that transboundary groundwater governance should be organized around the geography of groundwater use and potential cross-border interactions rather than treating shared aquifers as uniform governance units.

items.title: Identification and characterization of neoplastic cells in keratin-positive giant cell–rich tumors
items.summary_raw: Keratin-positive giant cell–rich tumor (KPGCT) is a newly described bone and soft tissue tumor. The tumor is characterized by scattered keratin-positive cells and the presence of HMGA2::NCOR2 fusions. It is not known if the HMGA2::NCOR2 fusion is located in the keratin-positive cells, and little is known about how KPGCT develops. KPGCT shares some histologic features with tenosynovial giant cell tumor (TGCT), a soft tissue tumor with CSF1 rearrangements. Single-nuclei RNA sequencing and Xenium spatial transcriptomics were used to elucidate the most likely mechanisms driving KPGCT and compare KPGCT to TGCT. We identified a population of cells coexpressing keratin, HMGA2 , and CSF1 as the likely neoplastic cells; these cells constitute the minority of the cells in the tumor. These cells express no synovial markers, confirming KPGCT as a distinct entity, separate from TGCT. The bulk of the tumor consists of CSF1R -expressing macrophages and multinucleated giant cells (MNGCs), suggesting an important role for CSF1–CSF1R signaling. In addition, we find that the likely neoplastic cell population shows activation of the hippo signaling pathway, a possible central pathway in KPGCT tumorigenesis. The CSF1–CSF1R axis likely stimulates the migration and proliferation of macrophages, which form the majority of cells in the tumor, as well as their differentiation into MNGCs. These results provide a rationale for the use of CSF1R inhibitors, which have already shown efficacy in TGCT, as a…

items.title: The World’s First Subsea Geothermal Well Had 8.7 Seconds of Glory
items.summary_raw: About 300 miles off the Oregon coast, a mile beneath the ocean’s surface, a startup just drilled the world’s first subsea geothermal well. And for a grand total of exactly 8.7 seconds, its prototype power plant generated about 2 kilowatts of net power. It wasn’t quite the result the Seattle-based Endurance Energy was hoping for — the company’s goal was to run its 100-kilowatt generator for a full year. But it’s not nothing. “We really proved with this mission that a geothermal well could be drilled and completed on the seafloor, and doing that within 21 months of the company existing I think is really a testament to our pace of progress,” Endurance CEO Andrew Redd told me. A former SpaceX engineer — as so many climate tech founders seem to be — Redd appears quite comfortable with the rapid trial-and-error cycles that hard tech startups often demand. Or as he stated in the company’s press release , which provides a refreshingly frank account of what this first test did and didn’t accomplish, “We follow the adage ‘make it exist, then make it good.’” Investors seem to be buying it. In June, the startup raised a $54 million Series A , led by Peter Thiel’s Founders Fund — Endurance’s second funding round in less than two years of existence. Still, the team certainly has their work cut out for them. The ocean is a notoriously difficult operating environment: Saltwater is corrosive and offshore infrastructure is difficult and expensive to build, maintain, and repair. Indeed…

The world is crumbling in ‘The History of Concrete’
items.summary_raw: It’s the second-most used material on Earth, it’s an environmental disaster, and it’s falling apart all around us. Meet concrete, the subject of a new feature-length documentary by John Wilson, a filmmaker with a knack for finding laugh-out-loud absurdity in the mundane. The History of Concrete stitches together quick cuts of handheld footage and deadpan narration in the same style as How To with John Wilson , the HBO show that made the filmmaker’s career. As in his episodes on “how to make small talk” and “how to put up scaffolding,” the titular subject of the film isn’t really the point. Instead, Wilson uses the theme of concrete as a kind of connective tissue, taking the viewer on a sprawling exploration of the overlooked corners of our world. Concrete’s pervasiveness allows this film to venture anywhere — a family-run mortuary that specializes in tattoo preservation, a patriotic brick-laying competition in Las Vegas, and a 3,100-mile spiritual race in which runners circle a single block in Queens for weeks on end. It would be a stretch to call the documentary a climate film. (In fact, it’s explicitly styled like a Hallmark movie.) But with each turn of the lens, Wilson sheds light on an unfolding environmental disaster. After all, he points out, concrete is the third biggest contributor to global warming . And although concrete is an indispensable part of modern life, its short, crumbling lifespan makes it a hazard on an increasingly disaster-prone planet. (Reader…

items.title: Expert perspectives on framing risk in engineering biology: anticipating ethical discourse about climate change mitigation
items.summary_raw: Abstract Given the rapid acceleration of the climate crisis, the IPCC has deemed Carbon Dioxide Removal (CDR) technologies as unavoidable to sufficiently mitigate the crisis. In this context, engineering biology (EngBio) is increasingly gaining traction in CDR research. While the deployment of EngBio is perceived by some as inherently high-risk for society, the economy, and the environment, the risks posed by insufficiently abated climate change are likely to be irreparable. Against this background, a pilot study was conducted, aimed at exploring experts’ perspectives on risk in decision-making regarding the use of advanced EngBio applications to develop CDR technologies. Our results show that EngBio experts are moderately or highly open to discussing, accepting, or taking the risks of using EngBio-based CDR. Our findings also indicate expert trust in the potential of rapid advancements in EngBio-based CDR technologies. While these findings do not entail an unconditional and uncritical acceptance of all risks arising from using EngBio for CDR purposes, they underscore a notion of risk as integral to environmental responsibility, namely as necessary to avoid the higher risk of insufficiently abated climate change. This study provides an integrated assessment of household energy expenditures and multidimensional energy poverty in Poland, combining long-term expenditure trends, energy consumption profiles, and socioeconomic determinants. Using nationally representative data from the Polish Household Budget Survey (Statistics Poland), we apply trend and elasticity analysis, k-means cluster analysis, and logistic regression to identify expenditure patterns, construct a multidimensional Energy Poverty (EP) index, and determine the factors associated with energy poverty risk. Cluster analysis reveals two dominant expenditure profiles (electricity–gas and district heating), differentiated by place of residence, income, and education; a small solid-fuel profile is identifiable only in 2023. Regression results show that energy poverty arises from the interaction of economic, social, and housing-related factors rather than low income alone. items.title: Improved Estimates of Equilibrium Climate Sensitivity From Non‐Equilibrated Climate Simulations
items.summary_raw: Abstract Calculating equilibrium climate sensitivity (ECS) requires simulations of a thousand years or more for the climate to re‐establish equilibrium, but most ECS estimates are derived from shorter model integrations. The widely used “Gregory method” for such estimates systematically underestimates ECS, a bias previously attributed to the time‐dependence of climate feedbacks. Here we demonstrate this underestimate instead arises primarily from an underestimate of radiative forcing. We present a modified method that corrects for the underestimate in forcing, producing ECS estimates that closely align with results from “long‐run” millennium‐scale simulations. This method is robust across models and offers an easily obtainable estimate of ECS with significantly higher accuracy. It enables reliable ECS estimates for full CMIP model ensembles, including models without millennium‐scale simulations. Using this method, we show one of every three CMIP6 climate models has an ECS greater than 5K—the upper bound of the “very likely” range in prior assessments. To further verify this method, we introduce an “integrated feedback parameter” which provides a more physically‐meaningful way to average a time‐evolving climate sensitivity by weighting the differential feedback in consecutive, non‐overlapping time segments by the fraction of energy imbalance that each segment restores. This parameter agrees well with that derived from our modified method, lending further credibility to this…
