Among the school-climate dimensions, Directiveness showed a positive unique association with PCI (β = .119). Differences were also observed according to professional seniority and disciplinary field. Overall, the findings indicate that PCI is associated primarily with educators’ educational beliefs, while perceived organizational conditions provide an additional but comparatively…

items.title: DIGITAL CLIMATE COMMUNICATION AND PUBLIC PERCEPTION: EXPLORING THE INFLUENCE OF SOCIAL MEDIA ON CLIMATE CHANGE DISCOURSE
items.summary_raw: Social media has transformed how the public at large perceives, debates and communicates about climate change. But the empirical evidence on how characteristics of digital climate communication translate to public perception and action is still limited and is dispersed. This study proposes and tests an integrated model of Social Media Exposure (SME), Information Credibility (IC), Engagement with Climate Content (ECC) and Peer Influence (PI) as antecedents of Public Perception of Climate Change (PPCC) which in turn results in Behavioural Intention (BI) to pro-environmental action based on the principles of the media effects theory, elaboration likelihood model and the climate change risk perception framework. The instrument used was a 28 item validated likert scale in a cross sectional survey of 315 active social media users. Reliability results ranged from .823 to .902 and multiple regression revealed that four antecedents accounted for 73.8% of the variance in PPCC (R² = .738, F(4, 310) = 218.63, p < .001); Engagement (β = .397) was the strongest predicting antecedent, followed by Peer Influence (β = .284), Social Media Exposure (β = .203), and Information Credibility (β = .178). Public Perception also predicted Behavioural Intention (BI) with a coefficient of β = .778 and R² = .606. The subgroups differed significantly by age group and primary platform, but not by gender. The findings show that it is not a passive exposure, but participatory engagement that is the key to…

items.title: Morecambe Area Gaming Environment (MAGE): An Applied Case Study for Coastal Futures and Adaptations
items.summary_raw: Large regions and coastal urban communities face significant climate-related risks, including coastal and river flooding, inundations, and sea-level rise. However, long-term predictions of coastal flooding, coastal change, and associated risks involve uncertainties that are difficult to communicate to those affected. This, in turn, can hinder the adaptation of coastal communities to future changes. In our proof-of-concept case study, MAGE (Morecambe Area Gaming Environment), we developed five research tools to enhance engagement between local government and local residents on coastal change, its effects on settlements, and the existing shoreline management plan (SMP) policies. First, we created an open community mapping platform to gather voluntary geographic information (VGI). Second, we developed a mini tabletop game for KS3 Geography for secondary schools. Third, a serious tabletop game that simulates coastal systems and places in North-West UK, playing with communities and schools as a precursor to informing and developing the fourth tool: a sandbox computing system. The portable digital chessboard sandbox that visualises thousands of what-if scenarios in 2055 and 2105 uses Lancaster University’s high-end computing (HEC) resources and a VR experience (our fifth tool). This article concentrates on the decision table, using numerical coastal models, GIS, and algorithms ported to a game engine; the MAGE system features interactive play pieces that the public can move in a…

items.title: Climate Justice in Sub‐Saharan Africa: Unequal Burdens and Pathways to Socially Just Adaptation
items.summary_raw: ABSTRACT Climate change in Sub‐Saharan Africa is often framed through vulnerability, resilience, and adaptation, yet these concepts alone do not fully explain the unequal social, economic, and political conditions shaping climate harm. This review examines climate change through a climate justice lens, focusing on unequal burdens, household welfare losses, fiscal constraints, adaptation finance, gendered inequalities, and pathways to socially just adaptation. Using a structured integrative review, the study synthesizes 52 sources, including 46 peer‐reviewed journal articles and selected institutional and policy reports used mainly for regional statistics and climate‐finance architecture. The findings show that climate injustice operates across interconnected structural, community, and household levels. Historical responsibility, uneven development, debt, limited fiscal space, infrastructure deficits, and unequal access to finance constrain adaptation, while climate shocks reduce incomes, assets, consumption, food and water security, health, and livelihoods. These effects vary across subregions and are differentiated by gender, class, age, location, livelihood systems, and institutional access. The review argues that socially just adaptation requires context‐sensitive financing instruments, meaningful local participation, gender‐responsive institutions, adaptive social protection, recognition of local and Indigenous knowledge, and measurable accountability to ensure…

items.title: Integrated, adaptive decarbonization strategies for last mile delivery
items.summary_raw: The aim of this study is to identify and assess the importance of selected decarbonization instruments in shaping integrated, adaptive, and low-emission last-mile delivery strategies, taking into account consumer behavioural determinants. The study utilised a modelling approach, developing a conceptual model integrating regulatory, organisational, and behavioural factors, which was then subjected to preliminary empirical verification. The obtained results indicate that the decarbonization process is nonlinear and systemic, based on interdependencies between the regulatory, strategic, and consumer levels. Regulatory pressure and enterprise adaptation strategies play a key role, significantly determining operational efficiency and the implementation of low-emission solutions, while the influence of behavioural factors remains relatively limited. Consequently, the research hypothesis was partially confirmed, indicating an asymmetry in the interactions between ”top-down” and ”bottom-up” mechanisms. A limitation of the study is the need for further in-depth empirical verification, particularly using operational data and a broader consideration of the demand side. Practical implications include the need to develop integrated adaptation strategies, intensify digitalisation processes, and apply behavioural economics tools to logistics demand management. In the social dimension, the importance of strengthening the role of consumers in the low-carbon transition process is emphasised…

items.title: Urban cooking in the global south: Social dimensions, urgency, and climate mitigation potential
Beyond trade facilitation: how China’s cross-border e-commerce pilot zones improve urban carbon efficiency
items.summary_raw: Background Digital trade may support lower-carbon economic development. Its environmental benefits depend on the balance between efficiency gains and the energy and logistics demands of trade expansion. Existing research links cross-border e-commerce pilot zones to urban carbon emission efficiency, but the conditions under which these gains arise need closer examination. Objectives This study examines whether cross-border e-commerce pilot zone designation improves urban carbon emission efficiency. It also explores potential transmission channels and assesses differences by geographic region, digital infrastructure, and environmental regulation. Methods We use 2010–2022 panel data for Chinese cities, with 3,666 city–year observations in the baseline regressions, to estimate a staggered difference-in-differences model of Cross-Border E-Commerce Pilot Zone (CEPZ) designation. Carbon emission efficiency is measured with a super-efficiency slacks-based measure (SBM) incorporating undesirable outputs. The model controls for population, economic development, urbanization, fiscal expenditure intensity, financial development, and higher education resources. Standard errors are clustered at the city level. Event-study, placebo, and Sun–Abraham analyses assess robustness alongside alternative specifications, including two-way clustering by province and year and one-way clustering by province. We examine three potential mechanisms and test coefficient differences using bdiff bootstrap…

items.title: Impact of Economic, Energy and Climate Policy Uncertainties on Multiple Energy Transition Pathways
items.summary_raw: ABSTRACT Achieving net‐zero and sustainable energy goals requires policy frameworks resilient to economic, energy and climate policy uncertainty. This study examines how these uncertainties, alongside globalisation, capital intensity and environmental regulatory stringency, shape three energy transition pathways across OECD countries (1991–2020): the shift from dirtier to less‐dirty non‐renewable sources (DLD), the shift from clean‐to‐cleaner renewable sources (CMC), and a comprehensive energy transition index (CET) combining both. Using the Fully Modified Ordinary Least Squares (FMOLS) estimator to address endogeneity and estimate long‐run co‐integrating relationships, the study finds that climate policy uncertainty is associated with DLD but not with CMC and CET, suggesting it redirects rather than accelerates the transitions. World economic and energy‐related uncertainty exert pathway‐specific effects that vary across the three measures. Globalisation and environmental regulatory stringency emerge as robust, positive drivers of all three pathways. Capital intensity supports the CMC and CET pathways but not DLD, suggesting capital‐intensive investment accelerates renewable deployment more than it improves the non‐renewable energy mix. Economic growth shows a similarly divergent effect, reducing the DLD transition while promoting CMC and CET, reflecting its dual role in reinforcing fossil‐fuel infrastructure and financing cleaner alternatives. These findings carry…

items.title: Politics of Climate Regime and Access to Climate Justice: An Analysis from the Perspective of Third World Approach to International Law
items.summary_raw: Climate change is one of the most urgent and complex challenges confronting the global community today, yet international legal and political responses remain fragmented and deeply unequal. Despite extensive negotiations under the international climate regime, the divide between developed and developing nations continues to shape outcomes that disadvantage the Global South. While the impacts of climate change—rising sea levels, food and water insecurity, severe weather events, and forced migration—fall disproportionately on vulnerable populations, international frameworks often prioritise the interests of powerful industrialised states. This article examines the political dynamics of the climate regime through the lens of the Third World Approach to International Law (TWAIL), demonstrating how structural inequalities, rooted in historical injustices, limit equitable access to climate justice. Drawing on the TWAIL framework, it critically analyses the shift from the principle of “common but differentiated responsibilities” under the Kyoto Protocol to the flexible model of “nationally determined contributions” in the Paris Agreement, highlighting how this transformation diluted accountability and eroded the obligations of developed states to provide financial, technological, and infrastructural support to developing countries. Special attention is given to contested areas such as loss and damage funding, climate finance, and technology transfer, where promises often fall short…

items.title: Study on the Action Path of Environmental Communication in Urban Residents' Residential Choice Under the Mediation of Policy Perception
items.source_name: Frontiers in Humanities and Social Sciences
items.summary_raw: This paper studies the effect of environmental communication on the choice of place for urban residents through policy perception. It will not provide new empirical data, but it will collect related studies on environmental media coverage, risk communication and residential location choices to build a conceptual action plan. First, this paper will introduce how agenda-setting and framing in environmental journalism affect public attention and risk perception; then, it will examine the connection between these perceptions and institutional trust and awareness of environmental and housing policies. Based on research into air pollution perception, information consumption behaviour and preferences for environmental amenities in cities, this paper puts forward that policy perception may moderate the relationship between environmental communication and residents' evaluations of neighbourhood quality, environmental justice and future risk. The new system thinks that the messages of environmental responsibility released by the government and local authorities will affect people's decisions to move. Therefore, in the Design of communication strategies and urban policies, we need to take a mediating path; we should not focus too much on the effect of media messages and recognise that they also shape people's perceptions of environmental quality and living conditions.

items.title: Scenario-Based Planning for Hydrogen Infrastructure and Trade in Nigeria: Navigating Policy, Technology, and Sustainability Uncertainties
items.source_name: INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF ENGINEERING AND MODERN TECHNOLOGY
items.summary_raw: The global transition to a low-carbon economy has positioned hydrogen as a critical energy carrier, offering Nigeria—with its abundant natural gas reserves, vast solar potential, and established energy infrastructure—a strategic opportunity to lead Africa’s hydrogen economy. This study develops a scenario framework to address uncertainties and opportunities in Nigeria’s hydrogen infrastructure and trade, aligning with its Energy Transition Plan and Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). Through a mixed-methods approach, including stakeholder engagement and literature review, the paper evaluates three hydrogen production pathways: green (renewable-based), blue (natural gas with carbon capture), and grey (conventional gasbased). Each pathway presents distinct trade-offs in cost, emissions, and infrastructure requirements. The analysis identifies key drivers—technological advancements, policy support, and infrastructure investment—and constructs four plausible scenarios using an impact-uncertainty matrix: Hydrogen Leap (high policy/tech), Policy-Led Delay (high policy/low tech), Tech-Driven Push (low policy/high tech), and Business as Usual (low policy/tech). These scenarios assess Nigeria’s potential as a hydrogen exporter to Europe, Asia, and West Africa, considering regional demand, infrastructure readiness, and geopolitical dynamics. A SWOT analysis further highlights Nigeria’s strengths (e.g., gas reserves, solar resources) and challenges (e.g., funding gaps, policy…

items.title: Sectoral structure and corporate climate strategy: A typology of adaptation, mitigation and ambidextrous configurations in emerging economies
items.source_name: International Journal of Business and Management (IJBM)
items.summary_raw: Research on corporate climate strategy usually explains differences in decarbonisation through managerial cognition, leadership, capabilities or institutional pressure. This paper develops a complementary meso-level explanation: sectoral structural attributes, namely risk exposure profile, asset-cycle longevity and institutional context, filter macro-level climate pressures and condition the feasible set of firm-level responses. Using an integrative review that combines 52 peer-reviewed studies identified through Scopus and Web of Science, 12 institutional reports and 22 corporate disclosures (2021–2024), the study compares agribusiness, renewable energy and heavy manufacturing, with India as the principal context. It develops three ideal types. The Resilient Adapter is shaped by immediate physical risk and favours adaptation. The Transformative Mitigator is shaped by transition opportunity and climate-aligned capital and favours mitigation-led growth. The Ambidextrous Navigator is shaped by long-lived carbon-intensive assets and contested institutional pressure, and sustains legacy operations while investing selectively in low-carbon alternatives. Structural contingency theory supplies the fit logic, socio-technical transitions and institutional theory explain meso-level conditions, dynamic capabilities explain variation in execution, and configuration theory guides ideal-type construction. The paper proposes that the gap between climate disclosure and action varies with…

items.title: PERCEPTIONS OF SOCIAL-ENVIRONMENTAL DISTURBANCE RELATE TO CLIMATE CHANGE ALONG A TROPICAL ESTUARY IN BRAZIL 7° SOUTH
items.source_name: Revista Ibero-Americana de Humanidades, Ciências e Educação
items.summary_raw: Climate crisis is the main contemporary environmental problem haunting everyone, especially the poor regions in the poorest countries. It subjects the human being to multiple and complex challenges, mainly related to means of subsistence in occupation of coastal territories, exposing poor communities to conditions of extreme vulnerability. The objective of this work is to evaluate the perception of fishermen, managers, specialists and lay people about social vulnerabilities imposed by climate change and sea level rise in the Paraiba-Brazil coastal and estuarine environment in 2017 and up to 2050. The research used a qualitative-quantitative approach to describe and analyse different actors, relating social problems influenced by climate change impacts: on housing prices, coastal and estuarine communities’ migration, health and wellbeing, violence and if something is being done to enhance the adaptive capacity. 73% of those who have institutional power think that in 2050 beach houses will have greater value. However, 75% of them expect that by 2050 coastal communities close to water will be removed, causing and stirring up various types of conflicts, as well as financial losses. The fishermen communities, however, are far more concerned. Every single respondent expects rising rates of violence due to a hostile environment.

items.title: Cognitive Abilities, Personality, and Sustainable Attitudes and Behavior
items.summary_raw: Climate change demands urgent action, yet individual engagement in sustainable behaviors remains inconsistent. We conducted two studies (N 1 = 280, N 2 = 973) examining how political orientation, personality traits, reasoning ability, social-emotional-behavioral skills, and complex problem solving relate to sustainable attitudes and behaviors in U.S. adults. Using structural equation modeling, we found that openness to experience was the strongest predictor, alongside liberal political orientation and self-perceived social engagement and innovation skills. Unexpectedly, both cognitive personality traits showed negative associations with sustainability outcomes, challenging the notion that cognitive abilities universally facilitate adaptive behavior. For sustainable behavior, these associations were small to moderate (−.25 ≤ r ≤ −.15) and most pronounced for food-related and engagement-related behaviors. Specification curve analyses confirmed that less established constructs (social, emotional, and behavioral skill self-concepts and complex problem solving) contributed meaningful variance beyond established personality predictors and that these associations were robust across analytical specifications. Overall, psychological characteristics together explained up to 44% of variance in sustainable attitudes and 29% of variance in sustainable behavior. These findings advance our understanding of the psychological underpinnings of environmental engagement and highlight the need…

items.title: When shocks enter the home: Household energy insecurity and compound vulnerability in emerging economies
items.summary_raw: Climate hazards can turn inadequate housing, insecure household energy services, and limited recovery finance into lasting welfare losses. However, research on climate vulnerability, energy poverty, housing precarity, and household risk management seldom examines how these conditions interact within the home. We develop an integrative conceptual synthesis of these four research streams, focusing on low- and middle-income countries. The synthesis distinguishes climatic hazards from the resulting disruptions to services, prices, and livelihoods, and explains how dwelling quality, effective energy services, and financial coping capacity influence harm and recovery. We derive five ideal-typical vulnerability regimes, namely resilient but exposed, energy-constrained, shelter-constrained, repair-constrained, and compound-vulnerability households. The first three describe structural positions, the fourth identifies a realised failure of post-shock recovery, and the fifth reflects interacting constraints. Financial fragility can exist before a shock without establishing that recovery has failed. We set out an empirical approach that separates pre-shock conditions, subsequent coping responses, and later welfare outcomes. The framework explains why interventions addressing only energy, housing, or finance may leave households vulnerable when another constraint remains unresolved. It also offers testable implications for household panel research and for designing interventions suited…

items.title: From waste to resilience: the future of wastewater
items.source_name: Critical Insights in Environmental Science and Technology
items.summary_raw: Global water scarcity, influenced by climate change, population increase, and the exhaustion of freshwater resources, requires wastewater recycling. This article emphasizes the importance of wastewater within a circular and climate-resilient economy that functions as a source of clean water, fertilizers, and energy. The Critical Insights research suggests that future wastewater treatment facilities should be designed using sustainable technologies with minimal energy requirements to increase the percentage of treated wastewater worldwide. Effluent from current wastewater plants contribute to eutrophication, so increased nutrient removal and recovery are needed. Persistent contaminants like heavy metals, PFAS, and microplastics accumulate in biosolids, complicating their use as biofertilizers in agriculture. Aquaculture wastewater has lower levels of recalcitrant contaminants, providing opportunities for testing new technologies and generating biosolids suitable for beneficial use. Using wastewater as a resource to support aquaculture and flood prevention may catalyze improved wastewater treatment. Restoring ecological balance, enhancing global food and water security, and establishing a just, regenerative, and climate-resilient circular economy require the integration of pollution removal, nutrient recycling, and renewable energy production in wastewater treatment.

items.title: Clustering European Union Countries by Energy Diversity, Economic Performance and Energy-Related Emission Intensity
items.source_name: International Journal of Engineering and Management Sciences
items.summary_raw: Sustainable and diversified energy production is an important challenge in today’s energy economics; nevertheless, the literature in this field is insufficient. This study aims to examine the energy-related greenhouse gas (GHG) emission intensity, GDP per capita, and energy diversity of the 27 Member States of the European Union in 2024, using cluster analysis and cluster validation indices like Silhouette, Calinski–Harabasz, and Davies–Bouldin, to explore whether the countries form statistically distinguishable groups and to explore the relationship between the variables. Spearman's rank correlation revealed a strong, significant negative relationship between GDP per capita and energy-related emissions intensity, i.e., more economically developed countries are typically characterised by lower energy-related emissions intensity. In contrast, GDP per capita was not significantly related to energy diversity, suggesting that economic development alone does not determine energy diversification. The results show that EU Member States follow different decarbonisation paths. The cluster with the most energy diversity, Bulgaria, the Czech Republic and Poland, has the highest energy-related emissions intensity, suggesting that a diversified energy mix based on fossil and nuclear sources does not reduce emissions on its own. In contrast, the cluster consisting of only two countries, Ireland and Luxembourg, is characterised by low energy-related emissions intensity despite their high…

items.title: Coaching Climate and Decisions Under Competitive Pressure: Autonomy Support, Psychological Safety, and Attentional Control in Athletes
items.source_name: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
items.summary_raw: Coaches influence the interpersonal and informational environments in which athletes learn, respond to mistakes and make decisions under competitive pressure. This critical integrative narrative review examines the proposed links among achievement-goal climate, autonomy-supportive coaching, basic psychological need satisfaction, communication and attention during demanding sport situations. It distinguishes task-focused feedback from personal evaluation, autonomy support from permissiveness, and decision quality from the eventual competitive result. Syntheses of coach-athlete motivation and athlete well-being provide evidence for associations between need support, autonomous motivation and adaptive experience; experimental work on pressure-sensitive skilled performance offers narrower mechanistic hypotheses. The article develops a conditional four-stage model in which coaching context influences situation-specific appraisal and information sharing, potentially affecting attentional allocation and observable choice. It also considers relevant alternatives, including technical expertise, fatigue, team structure, tactical constraints and reverse causation. No original participants, causal intervention results or pooled estimates are presented. Proposed tests include independent observation of coaching, repeated event-level decisions, preregistered multilevel analyses, matched active-control interventions and external replication. Practical applications emphasize clear…
authors: Özduru Assoc. Prof. Dr. Ocak Korhan

items.title: Investors' ideology and corporate symbolic and substantive climate actions
items.summary_raw: Abstract Research Summary Prior research suggests that institutional investors' liberalism is associated with firms' engagement in environmental sustainability, yet whether this association manifests in symbolic or substantive actions remains unclear. Taking a question‐driven approach, our analyses of Russell 3000 firms (2010–2020) reveal that investor liberalism, measured as the proportion of donations made to the Democratic Party, is positively associated with symbolic climate actions only from 2016 onward (a period when political polarization intensified), reversing a negative association during 2010–2015. Its positive association with substantive actions from 2016 onward, however, appears only among consistent Democratic donors (stronger liberal values), among dedicated investors, or in firms without CEO duality (greater investor influence). These findings indicate that liberal investor ownership may encourage, rather than deter, firms' environmental decoupling. Managerial Summary Liberal institutional investors tend to favor greater corporate environmental sustainability efforts, but are they associated with firms' symbolic or substantive climate actions? Our findings based on U.S. firms reveal that across the full 2010–2020 period, firms with more liberal investors, as indicated by their Democratic‐leaning political donations, do not exhibit more symbolic or substantive climate actions. From 2016 onward, as political polarization intensified, firms with more liberal…

items.title: Tariff Uncertainty and Climate Imperatives: Strategies for Supply Chain Decarbonization in Asia
items.summary_raw: As low-carbon manufacturing accelerates, Asian export economies face growing pressure from cross-border carbon rules and unilateral trade tariffs. Mechanisms such as the European Union’s Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM), together with rising protectionism, have made supply chain emissions central to market access and competitiveness. This paper examines how tariff volatility interacts with climate mandates across Asian production networks and assesses three strategies: carbon-pricing alignment, regional value chain integration, and clean energy deployment in industrial clusters. It finds that without shared carbon accounting standards and transition finance; fragmented border measures may widen industrial disparities between advanced and developing Asian economies. The study highlights the need for cooperative trade-climate frameworks that balance competitiveness with deep decarbonisation across ASEAN and South East Asia.

items.title: Green manures and crop residues for soil fertility restoration in paddy-based cropping systems of monsoon Asia: balancing carbon sequestration and greenhouse gas emissions
items.summary_raw: Paddy-based cropping systems are the foundation of crop production in monsoon Asia, but their long-term sustainability is increasingly compromised by soil organic carbon depletion and declining soil nitrogen fertility, particularly where paddy fields are converted to upland use for wheat, soybean, and other crops. Green manures have long been used as on-farm sources of organic matter and biologically fixed nitrogen, but their role is being re-evaluated in the context of reduced fertilizer dependence, soil fertility restoration, and climate change mitigation. This review summarizes studies since the 1970s on the agronomic characteristics and utilization of green manure crops in paddy-based systems of monsoon Asia, with particular attention to Chinese milk vetch, hairy vetch, Sesbania, Crotalaria, green manure soybean, and Azolla. The integrated use of green manures with rice straw and other crop residues is examined as a strategy for maintaining soil organic carbon, enhancing nitrogen self-support capacity, and improving the resilience of rice-upland rotations. Finally, greenhouse gas trade-offs associated with organic matter incorporation, especially methane emissions under flooded conditions and nitrous oxide emissions under aerobic or intermittently aerobic conditions, are discussed. Although low-C/N leguminous green manures can partially replace synthetic nitrogen fertilizers and synchronize nitrogen release with crop demand, high-C/N residues such as rice straw are…

items.title: Beyond barriers: perceived barriers and winter sport participation intentions in a predominantly Zhejiang-based Chinese sample
items.summary_raw: Background Following China's national strategy to promote winter sports, understanding the psychological mechanisms driving participation among residents in China's Yangtze River Delta region—a population with limited traditional exposure to ice and snow activities—has become increasingly important. This study integrated the Theory of Planned Behavior (TPB) with leisure constraint theory and self-efficacy theory to examine how perceived barriers were associated with winter sport participation intentions through attitudinal and behavioral control pathways, and whether self-efficacy moderates these relationships. Methods A cross-sectional online survey was conducted with 415 self-identified residents of southern China. Structural equation modeling was employed to test the hypothesized relationships among perceived barriers, attitude, subjective norm, perceived behavioral control (PBC), self-efficacy, and participation intention. Bootstrap mediation analysis was used to assess indirect effects, and moderation analysis was performed to examine the conditional role of self-efficacy. Results Perceived barriers demonstrated significant positive associations with both attitude (β = 0.16, p = 0.001) and PBC (β = 0.32, p < 0.001), a pattern consistent with constraint negotiation theory. Among the TPB predictors, PBC (β = 0.23, p < 0.001) and subjective norm (β = 0.20, p = 0.007) both significantly predicted participation intention, while attitude did not reach statistical significance…

items.title: Rare diseases are an overlooked dimension in climate–health adaptation
items.summary_raw: Nature Climate Change, Published online: 19 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41558-026-02770-2 A resilient society must prepare not only for common harms but also for uncommon vulnerabilities, such as rare disease where the consequences leave no room for failure. Ensuring that people with rare diseases have reliable access to essential care is crucial for fairness and safety in a changing climate.

items.title: Populist opposition to climate policy: the role of policy design
items.summary_raw: Populist actors increasingly pressure policymakers to navigate a trade-off between effective climate policy and its public feasibility. However, one may ask whether a populist worldview is inherently more opposed to some types of climate policies than to others, and if so, why? An emerging literature has found populist citizens oppose climate policies writ large. Building on this literature, we argue that populist citizens do not oppose all climate policies to the same extent. Differentiating climate change policies based on their policy design, we hypothesise that populist citizens substantially reject climate policies more if they are ‘push’ measures, leverage market-based instruments or target ‘the people’. We test these arguments by utilising high-quality Austrian panel data. We find that populist citizens are indeed less supportive of climate policy, however, this relationship is moderated by policy design and independent from thick-ideological leanings. Populist backlash is particularly pronounced for policies that target individuals and leverage ‘push’ measures. Vice versa, policies targeting companies or employing incentivising measures face significantly less backlash. These findings suggest that policy design indeed can mitigate the populist backlash against climate policy and policymakers can utilise this evidence to create more robust climate policy packages.

items.title: Integrasi Pelabelan Inset Lexicon dan SVM untuk Klasifikasi Sentimen Doomscrolling di Tiktok
items.source_name: Jurnal Ilmu Komputer dan Sistem Komputer Terapan (JIKSTRA)
items.summary_raw: This study was motivated by rising public complaints regarding the habit of doomscrolling on social media, particularly TikTok, a practice often linked to negative impact on users mental health. Public opinion on this phenomenon has yet to be systematically mapped, especially given the informal and unstructured nature of TikTok comments. This research aims to analyze sentiment regarding the doomscrolling phenomenon through TikTok comments using a lexicon based approach. Data were collected by retrieving TikTok videos using the search terms “doomscrolling” and “TikTok addiction” via scraping techniques, followed by text preprocessing, automated sentiment labeling using the InSet Lexicon, feature extraction via Term Frequency Inverse Document Frequency (TF-IDF), and classification using the Support Vector Machine (SVM) algorithm. The results indicate that negative sentiment dominates at 70.72%, followed by neutral sentiment 16.57%, and positive sentiment at 12.71%. The classification model achieved an accuracy of 75.76%, a precision of 76.66%, a recall of 75.76%, and an F1-score of 76.07%. These findings suggest that public generally perceives doomscrolling as a troubling habit, and the developed model proves effective for mapping public opinion on the doomscrolling phenomenon on TikTok.

items.title: Community as a driver in macroalgae market development: the California Seaweed Festival case study
items.summary_raw: Environmental changes are affecting ecological systems, natural resource availability, and human production systems. Within this context, scientists and entrepreneurs are developing new approaches to production and resource use, including innovations in energy, clothing, packaging, food, and other sectors. As part of the effort to address these pressing issues, two phycologists created the California Seaweed Festival (CSF), an annual community outreach program entering its seventh year. The Festival promotes education about various aspects of macroalgae in a festive, informal, and experiential-learning environment. We document the evolution of this program over time, including changes in the Festival’s structure and funding model made to expand points of entry and levels of engagement. The Festival features representatives from the seaweed aquaculture industry and collaborating organizations showcasing their applications in food, drink, cosmetics, visual and performing arts, robotics, chemistry and materials, ecology, and kelp forest restoration. This broad program is motivated by ecological challenges and the challenges that the seaweed aquaculture industry has faced in securing social license to operate and in developing both the consumer- and producer-side of the market economy. To demonstrate how the Festival has worked to address those constraints, this case study includes results from interviews conducted with aquaculture industry professionals in 2025 and 2026, and a…

items.title: CONTEXTUALIZED CLIMATE RESILIENCE EDUCATION FRAMEWORK TO STRENGTHEN TEACHERS’ PEDAGOGICAL PRACTICES IN THE DIVISION OF AGUSAN DEL SUR
items.source_name: EPRA International Journal of Multidisciplinary Research (IJMR)
items.summary_raw: This study examined teachers' pedagogical practices, knowledge, attitudes, and competencies, as well as the challenges encountered in integrating climate resilience concepts in the Division of Agusan del Sur. Using a quantitative descriptive-correlational research design, the study involved 150 public secondary school teachers selected through stratified random sampling. Data were collected using a researcher-developed questionnaire and analyzed using weighted means and Pearson's correlation coefficient. Findings revealed that teachers' pedagogical practices were highly practiced (WM = 3.59), while their knowledge, attitudes, and competencies were highly evident (WM = 3.65). However, teachers encountered serious challenges in integrating climate resilience concepts (WM = 3.11), particularly the lack of professional development programs, limited training opportunities, and overloaded teaching responsibilities. Significantly low negative relationships were found between pedagogical practices and challenges (r = -.286, p = .001) and between teachers' knowledge, attitudes, and competencies and challenges (r = -.312, p < .001). These results suggest that stronger teacher capacity was associated with fewer reported challenges, although other institutional and contextual factors may also influence implementation. Based on the findings, a Contextualized Climate Resilience Education Framework was developed to strengthen teacher capacity, improve pedagogical practices, and address…

items.title: Banana (Musa spp.) Production Systems in Ethiopia- Challenges, Opportunities and Future Prospects: A Review
items.summary_raw: Banana (Musa sp.) is one of the most important horticultural crops in Ethiopia, contributing significantly to household nutrition, income generation and rural livelihoods. Despite its increasing importance, banana production remains constrained by interacting biotic, abiotic, socioeconomic and institutional factors, including pests and diseases, limited access to improved planting materials and cultivars, decline in soil fertility, weak value chains and increasing climate-related risks. This review synthesizes evidence on banana production systems, major production constraints, value-chain dynamics, opportunities and climate change in Ethiopia. The evidence indicates that banana production is predominantly smallholder-based, characterized by low input use, limited access to quality planting materials and inadequate agronomic management. Climate change and variability further exacerbate these challenges through rising temperatures, rainfall variability and extreme weather events, with implications for yield stability and pest and disease pressure. Nevertheless, Ethiopia’s diverse agroecological conditions provide opportunities for banana expansion under both rain-fed and irrigated systems. Improved cultivars, quality planting-material technologies, irrigation, climate-smart practices, strengthened research-extension systems and value addition offer important pathways to enhance productivity and resilience. The review highlights the need for coordinated investment in improved…

items.title: From Policy to Practice: The Attitude–Behaviour Gap in University Sustainability and its Implications for SDGs in Cameroon
items.summary_raw: This article interrogates the persistent gap between policy declarations in favour of sustainable development in Cameroonian higher education and the effective behaviours of students. By crossing empirical data gathered from 200 students at the University of Yaounde 1 with Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs 4, 7, 12 and 13), the study reveals that university policies, organizational cultures and daily practices do not significantly predict student behavioural competencies, whereas management strategies and knowledge devices do. This analysis suggests that Cameroon’s progress towards SDGs depends on closing a “governance bottleneck” separating normative declaration from structured action. The article argues for systemic integration of sustainability objectives into university governance as a necessary condition for transforming individual intentions into national contributions for 2030 and 2035 agendas.
